Mr. Speaker, it is a well known fact that United States law requires that the ownership of nuclear weapons must remain with the United States and that the use of such weapons requires presidential authorization. That is the law as it now stands and as it has been in effect since 1945 or 1946.
At the same time, as I have said before in the house, if and when nuclear weapons are acquired by the Canadian forces, these weapons will not be used except as the Canadian government decides and in the manner approved by the Canadian government. These two elements together constitute joint control, and joint control is consistent with the view I expressed in the house on February 20, 1959, that it is important to limit the spread of nuclear weapons at the independent disposal of national governments.
I think I should add this, that negotiations and consultations with the United States have been continuing for a very considerable time, and the reason for the continuance of the negotiations is in order to attain the objectives I pointed out in February, 1959, so that if and when an agreement is arrived

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING CURRENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government has been following with much concern the tragic developments which have led to internal strife and violence in the new republic of Congo. Reports on the situation are conflicting. Even at the present time there is no clear picture of what is actually happening, but it is apparent that the Congolese nation is facing a serious threat to its existence. There is need to bring about the restoration of law and order throughout the country, and the government of Congo has requested outside assistance to achieve this end. It goes without saying that the Congolese government must be the primary source of authority, and no outside power including the United Nations can or should assume that responsibility. All that can be done by other nations is to respond to reasonable requests for assistance.
On July 12 the secretary general of the United Nations received from the president and the prime minister of the Congo a cable resquesting the urgent dispatch of military assistance by the United Nations. This request was in addition to the Congolese request for technical assistance which had already been discussed between the Congolese authorities and Dr. Ralph Bunche, as I said two days ago.
The secretary general requested that the security council be convened on July 13. The council met last evening and until the early hours of this morning. The proceedings began with a statement by the secretary general on the steps which he envisaged as part of a United Nations program of assistance to the republic of the Congo.
The secretary general has emphasized that the difficulties in the Congo are connected with the maintenance of order and the protection of lives. The request for urgent technical assistance which had been made by Dr. Bunche in the field of administration was aimed especially at assistance in restoring the civil authority. This request is within the competence of the secretary general, and he has been considering steps to implement it including the secondment of some military

officers now serving with the United Nations truce supervisory organization in Palestine to service in the Congo.
To meet immediate needs, the secretary general considered it necessary to respond to the second Congolese request, that for military assistance. Notwithstanding the risks and difficulties, he believes that a United Nations stopgap arrangement through establishing in the Congo a United Nations force for restoring and maintaining order is preferable to any other formula for meeting the situation. His conclusion, which he conveyed to the security council, was that the United Nations should accede to the request of the Congo, and he strongly recommended that he be authorized to take the necessary steps.
This authorization was given by the council early this morning. A resolution submitted by Tunisia and reading in part as follows authorized the secretary general-
-to take the necessary steps in consultation with the government of the republic of Congo to provide the government with such military assistance as may be necessary until, through the efforts of the Congolese government with the technical assistance of the United Nations, the national security forces may be able, in the opinion of the government, to meet fully their tasks.
The resolution was adopted by a vote of 8 in favour, none against and 3 abstentions, China, France and the United Kingdom. The resolution also called upon Belgium to withdraw its troops from the Congo. It was the secretary general's understanding that if the United Nations were to act as he had proposed the Belgian government would see its way clear to withdrawing its forces.
The secretary general has said that arrangements for placing the military force in the Congo would be under way in a matter of hours. He has been consulting with member governments concerning the contingents for the proposed military force. It is his intention that they should be drawn mainly from African countries, and it is these countries which he is currently consulting. The house will recall that yesterday I pointed out that I felt that whs the proper course to be followed at this time, so as to place the Congolese under no misapprehension regarding the action taken by contingents mobilized from countries other than Africa.
At the same time the secretary general is proceeding with his plans for putting in motion the long term program of administrative assistance along the lines of the question asked a moment ago by the hon. member for Assiniboia. In particular, he is arranging for the temporary secondment of UNTSO officers and in an initial request has asked that Canada agree to the secondment of two Canadian officers. He has also been considering whether R.C.A.F. aircraft at present on duty 79951-0-396-J
Inquiries of the Ministry with UNEF should be used in this emergency for ferrying supplies and personnel to the Congo.
The government is responding favourably to requests of this kind because it believes that this is the most useful contribution which Canada can make in the current situation. If there are additional requests of the same nature they will be considered seriously.
The hon. gentleman asked me with regard to food. The United Nations reported that there is a very serious food shortage. Some governments have been approached about supplying foodstuffs. This is an area in which Canada might very well be able to make an effective contribution, and the government stands ready, to consider requests in that regard.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING CURRENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure hon. members will have listened with interest to the statement which the Prime Minister has made, and will certainly join him in approval of any action which the United Nations can take to restore this confused and almost anarchial situation, judging by reports, in the Congo.
I think it is important to provide technical, economic and administrative assistance to this new state. As a matter of fact I have always felt, as other hon. members have, that one of the most useful things the United Nations could do in current circumstances is to build up a corps of administrative experts which would be available for new states at the beginning of their existence, when administrative help of that kind is perhaps the help that would be most valuable to them. No doubt that is why Mr. Ralph Bunche was sent to the Congo in the first instance, but these things cannot be effective until order is restored. I think the United Nations has been correct in taking action in that field at once.
If there ever was a situation which underlines the necessity of having available a stand-by United Nations police force, ready, trained, equipped and with transportation so it could be moved into action at a moment's notice, this, Mr. Speaker, is it. In the light of these circumstances it is discouraging to realize that no progress has been made in recent years to build up that stand-by force. However, that being the situation, I think the United Nations through the secretary general and in compliance with the resolution of the security council, is doing everything presumably that can be done, and we can leave the matter with confidence in the hands of the secretary general who is acting with his usual speed and efficiency.
Although I think the Prime Minister is quite right in indicating that at this stage such police assistance might properly come

Inquiries of the Ministry from African nations to avoid any kind of misunderstanding, I hope if that kind of help is not available in the numbers that are required, or are presumed to be required, perhaps the government of Canada could let the United Nations know that we have a battalion trained, equipped and available for that kind of service that could be made available if it were required by the United Nations.

subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING CURRENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this is a day for renewed hope and justifiable pride in the action that is being taken by the United Nations. I think this is a strong indication of the effectiveness of the United Nations in preserving the peace of the world and in bringing order out of chaos in this emerging African nation. I am delighted with the action that has been taken by the security council. I express the hope that they will be able to raise the required police personnel within the bordering nations of Africa.
I think the Prime Minister was quite correct when he stated it would be preferable to have the United Nations police force composed of troops from neighbouring nations rather than to send white troops into that nation, which action might be misinterpreted. However, I know that Canadian troops are available if they are required in any way. I am sure all Canadians will support any effort that may be made by our country to provide technical assistance, food and necessary transportation in order to move personnel and supplies to this country.
I am confident that as this situation unfolds in the days ahead, peace and order will be restored, and that the citizens of this new nation will enjoy freedom and an improving standard of living. I am exceedingly pleased with the action taken by the United Nations security council, and I know that in any assistance the Canadian government is able to render the government in this instance will have the full support of the nation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on third reading of this bill to put forward a proposition which has been supported over the years by the C.C.F. party. We believe that the bill being discussed on third reading today is in general a good one, and contains many improvements as the result of the work of the committee on the Canada Elections Act. However, there is one particular feature of the bill that we should like to see changed, namely the provision as to the age of voters.
Throughout the bill it is provided that in order to be qualified as an elector a citizen must be of the full age of 21 years. We feel for many reasons that it would be helpful and that it would be a mark of progress and would receive the support of the Canadian people if the age of voters in this country could be reduced from 21 years to 18 years.
As the years go by it is well known to members in this house that young Canadians are getting a steadily improved education and are taking a growing and wider interest

Canada Elections Act
in public affairs. I do not think the knowledge of public afEairs of our 18 year olds today can really be compared with the knowledge of people of this age of 40 years ago or 50 years ago. The availability of mass communication, radio, television and newspapers, has made it possible for our young people to have an extremely wide knowledge of public affairs at an early age.
Our educational facilities in this country are being improved all the time. More and more young Canadians are availing themselves of these educational opportunities, so that as the years go by our young people are getting a steadily higher education. The 1911 census showed that 18 year olds in this country had on the average a grade 7 education. Thirty years later, with the 1941 census, the average education of young Canadians of the age of 18 had improved to the level of grade 10. Ten years later, at the 1951 census, it was shown that on the average young Canadians were in school for ten and a half years. I have no doubt that when the census is taken next year, once again a steady improvement in the education of our young people will be demonstrated.
We think it is quite an anomaly that many school teachers, when they first become qualified to teach school in this country, are in fact themselves under our present law too young to vote. Yet they have the qualifications that enable them to teach history, civics and social studies. In other words they are considered to be sufficiently qualified to impart their knowledge of public affairs to Canadian students, but we take the position or we have been taking the position as a parliament that they teach on these questions of public affairs but we do not think they have the suitability or the brain to cast an intelligent vote.
Some provinces have shown the federal government the lead. The province of Saskatchewan was the first province in Canada to lower the voting age to 18. In two other provinces, namely Alberta and British Columbia, the voting age has been lowered to 19. From practical experience, and from having taken part in election campaigns in provinces that have the lower voting age, I know that young people at the age of 18, 19 and 20 take a very active interest in election campaigns, in the discussion of public issues and in fact take sufficient interest to exercise their franchise. I might also say they are rather disturbed, frustrated and disappointed when a federal election being held a few months later denies to them under this kind of law the right to exercise their franchise in that election.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a just a word or two with regard to this amendment which would reduce the voting age in federal elections from 21 to 18. As the hon. gentleman who moved the amendment has pointed out, in the past the party which I now have the honour to lead has opposed this reduction in the voting age, and in the committee which considered this matter there was a division of opinion, I believe, among the Liberal members of that committee. There was at least one who advanced' some arguments against this change.
Perhaps this gives me an opportunity to reaffirm what I have said before, namely that because the Liberal party in the past did not take certain action that is no reason why its policies should not change as conditions may change. If I may paraphrase the words of Sir Winston Churchill, though they were applied to a different situation, we try to keep our party in harmonious concord with the development of events.
There is a great deal to be said in the circumstances of today for the reduction of the voting age from 21 to 18, and most of the major arguments in favour of such a change were given by the hon. member for As-siniboia. The argument which I think must make the greatest appeal is that we do not hesitate as a state to call on young people to fight for our country and, if necessary to die for our country, as thousands under the age of 21 have done. We ask them to accept the supreme obligation of citizenship in this regard, irrespective of whether they are 21 or 20 or 19 or 18, so it seems to me that if we ask Canadians to take on that obligation the time has come when they should have the privilege of voting so they

may do their share in determining the policies which might affect the situations in which they would be asked to share in this supreme obligation. I think young people of 18 or 19 or 20, as a result of the training they received in our educational establishments today, are quite qualified to use their judgment wisely and well in respect of the franchise as well as in respect of other matters on which we ask young people today to exercise their judgment.
We do place obligations on and grant privileges to young people in many fields now, including the privilege of paying taxes. If we are going to ask them to serve in the armed forces and to pay their share of the expenses of government, I think the time has come when we should give them the privilege of playing their part in determining government policy. So I think it is right that the voting age for this purpose should be reduced, all the more so because there have been changes in some of the provinces, though not in all of them, in regard to voting age. This is an indication of a trend. I agree with the hon. member that we should not wait until we have voting rules and regulations in all the provinces.
For these reasons, speaking as the leader of our party, I will be very happy to support the amendment which has been moved by the hon. member.

As a matter of fact I do not think any of the arguments on one side or the other of this matter are very strong. In spite of the eloquence of the hon. member for Assiniboia I do not think that Canada has not been a democracy because over the years people have not had a vote at age 18, nor do I think it will suddenly turn into a democracy if they do have a vote at that age. I think that kind of exaggeration does not really help very much in a discussion of important public affairs.
I think the most compelling argument is that emphasized by my hon. friend, the Leader of the Opposition, the argument that we accept people into the armed forces at age 18, and of course as long as they are on active service they do have the vote. All our regular armed forces have been on active service since 1950, so all of them have had the vote. All those who are liable to be immediately called upon to act in any sudden emergency have the vote now. I do not think there is any objection in principle, and I have never thought so, about giving the vote to people at the age of 18.
I said I was going to make a confession. I made it in the committee and I think I might just as well make it in the house. In any event I think the facts are pretty well known. At the age of 18 I was a hereditary Conservative; at the age of 21 I had seen the light and had become a Liberal. That is not an infrequent happening. It certainly was not unusual in the 1920's when it happened to me in western Canada. It was a very common experience. What was, of course, more unusual and more uncommon in western Canada in those years was another conversion of a much more distinguished member of the house than myself. While I was advancing another gentleman was receding. Of course I know it is not right to impute motives, so I will not attempt to identify the hon. member. It has always seemed to me that there is-perhaps it is a part of human nature-a tendency, once one has cast a vote, to become more identified with a political party than before one has cast a vote.

Mr. Speaker, having, at the committee, supported the amendment of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) with respect to lowering the age of electors from 21 years to 18 years, I think I should add a few remarks on the matter.
I think that, in stating that all Liberal members, save one, had voted in favour of the status quo, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) gave the house a wrong impression.
It is true that only two Liberal members were present at the committee, that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) voted with the majority, and that I voted with the member for Skeena, even supporting his amendment. This would indicate that 50 per cent of the Liberal members favoured the amendment, while the other 50 per cent opposed it. And if the Prime Minister seems to be somewhat shocked, as was the hon. member for Skeena, at the fact that today the Liberals seem inclined to approve the proposal to lower the voting age from 21 to 18, it is because he fails to understand the Liberal party, which stands for development and progress according to circumstances and needs. The Liberal party does not want to remain conservative, along the old principles and in the full sense of the word.
For my part, I have always favoured development and the right to vote at age 18 because, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) said a moment ago, since our young people can be compelled at 18 to risk their lives for their country, without even being consulted, they should at least have the right to express their opinion on that matter which decides their lives.
Furthermore, if young people at 18 are called upon to pay substantial taxes to the country, it seems to me they should have their say in the matter since they have to pay a substantial proportion of the country's expenses.
I quite perfectly understand what the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate means when he says that, had he been allowed to vote at age 18, he would probably have committed the monumental blunder of supporting the Conservative party, but that by the time he was 21 he had seen the light and had sided with a progressive party, the Liberal party.
I think there is another good reason in favour of the proposed change.
In 1926, radio and television were not nearly as developed as now, whereas today, after young people have left school, they can

supplement their education, and are therefore more able to express purely personal opinions. I contend that today more than ever, young men are prepared for the future, are entitled to express their opinions and to decide their own fate, especially in the event of a war, for it is not after our young people are in the armed forces that they can make their views known. It is before the government decides that our young people must go out and get killed that they have a right to have a hand in the choice of the government that will be taking the final decisions.
Those, Mr. Speaker, were my reasons for supporting the resolution of the hon. member for Skeena and that is why, again today, I am proud to join with my leader in openly supporting this progressive measure giving young people the right to decide their fate when opportunity offers.

Mr. Speaker, the question of the voting age was one of the major considerations of the committee that studied the Canada Elections Act. This point has been covered very thoroughly. Arguments on both sides were put forward and a motion was made which was defeated in the committee. As far as our party are concerned, we have had the privilege of listening to the Prime Minister briefly answer the leader of the C.C.F. party and the Leader of the Opposition, but we have not closed the door. The Prime Minister suggested that if it was desired at another session to have the committee investigate this particular matter he would be quite agreeable to this being done.
On the other hand, the C.C.F. leader has chosen to move this amendment at the very last minute of the consideration of this bill. The hon. member for Skeena tried to leave the impression that we had taken him by surprise the other day and had tried to force the bill down their throats, but there was absolutely nothing to prevent him moving this amendment when we were in committee on the bill. Therefore, even if we had wanted to lower the voting age, to do so at this stage would amount to a vote of non-confidence in the government, and we certainly cannot accept that.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a number of very good arguments have been advanced in favour of the amendment. It is not my wish to repeat them now, but one argument has not been presented about which I should like to speak very briefly.

I refer to the question of awareness of political activity and the political aspects of our national life. This is a very fundamental subject and one in which I know we are all very much interested. If it were possible by reducing the minimum age of electors to 18 from 21 to increase awareness of political affairs and encourage wider participation at an early age in political activity which would form a base for continued interest throughout the adult lives of such people, I think this change would be very worth while.
I have been particularly impressed by the students who have come here to visit parliament in session. High school and university students in their teens have shown an interest in and knowledge of the affairs of the house which I think would even put some members of the house to shame. Unfortunately I do not think this is true of all the young people of our country. In my opinion we should take all possible steps to encourage wider and deeper participation. Those who come from the maritime provinces, for example, know that among students there political awareness and activity are much keener and much more widespread than in the central provinces. At the University of Toronto interest in political activities and political party organizations is very small and is in fact minimal in proportion to the total enrolment in that great university. I think this situation is unfortunate, because it is an indication that the young people are not fully aware of and are not interested in the system which has made this country great.
Our party believe in the Liberal democratic system. We believe that the continuance of this system in the world is now subject to challenge. We are involved in a life and death struggle with another ideology, namely with the godless communist atheism which threatens to engulf us and our system. If our Liberal democratic system is going to survive it will require not only the participation of dedicated, informed and competent people to seek and hold public office, but also an informed and interested electorate at large.
If by lowering the voting age we could even to a small extent encourage a greater awareness and a wider participation, then I think this step would be worth while. Apathy is something that we must not encourage. Apathy permits abuse. Apathy opens the door to the disintegration of the parliamentary and the democratic system. If we can encourage our young people to participate in and to identify themselves with political movements, political ideas and political knowledge at an early age, I think this is a goal worthy of our
Canada Elections Act
support. For this reason, Mr. Speaker, I think those of us on this side of the house welcome the opportunity to express our feelings in this matter.
As was stated, we had on the order paper a bill which would do exactly the same thing as the amendment now before us. It has been some time since I have read the elections act, but I presume that if this amendment were carried and if the committee of the whole house made the change suggested, these young people would be able to seek election to this House of Commons at the age of 18. This possibility has been presented as one of the arguments against the adoption of such an amendment.
I am not sure that this would be a disadvantage. There is no reason why younger people should not present themselves for office when they would have their merits, their background and their qualifications for public office judged by the electorate at large on the same basis as those of their elders. It might even be that a few young people, a young ginger group in the House of Commons, would do something to the deliberations of this august body and present a leavening of new ideas which would make us even more aware than we have been of the tides of change.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, once again I should like to thank hon. members of all parties for the very friendly reception they have given me this afternoon as I commence to deal with the estimates of my department. This, I am sure, reflects the interest that all hon. members are taking in external affairs, and also reflects the fact that generally speaking there is a tripartisan attitude in the house in connection with the problems that come under the jurisdiction of this particular department.
In addition I should like to express thanks to those hon. members who served on the standing committee on external affairs. Once again that committee has done an excellent job, and hon. members this year have maintained the high standard which has been in existence from the start of that standing committee of the house.
I was also very much impressed by the interest taken by hon. members of the other house. They, too, have a committee on external affairs. I am not sure whether it is called the committee on external affairs or the committee on foreign relations, but in any event it deals with external affairs. They asked me to appear before that committee and we had a very helpful discussion.

Supply-External Affairs
I sometimes worry about the extent of the interest being taken in external affairs across the country. I am sure this thought must have occurred to one of my predecessors, the present Leader of the Opposition, from time to time. There are many complicated problems in the world today. Everyone has his or her own personal problems and is affected by problems in the home, the community and so on. One can understand why it must be a little difficult for large numbers of people to follow closely what goes on in international affairs; yet if a country is to take an active part in world affairs-certainly a country which is under a democratic type of government-it is vital that there be a wide awareness across the country of the different policies involved.
Canada, of course, has taken a very active part in foreign affairs for many years, and today is filing a role which is a great deal larger than one would expect of a nation with our population. I am very hopeful that in the years ahead this role will continue to grow. That means, of course, that the Canadian people and their representatives in parliament have rather a heavy obligation to endeavour to understand international problems and to create an informed public opinion. As I say, sometimes I am a little worried for fear that across the country there is not the interest being taken in foreign affairs that is essential if Canada is to maintain her place.
I wish to express a word of admiration for the members of my department. I include in that not only the foreign service officers but all the members of the department in the administrative branches and the clerical help. They are a group of Canadians who have a spirit of adventure. I think most of them are in the department because they are intrigued by the possibility of being posted abroad and of seeing something of the world. There is, I find, this spirit of adventure throughout the department.
It is not all pleasant for a foreign service officer or anyone else going abroad and taking his family overseas. The problem of the education of the children arises; how the children are to be sent to school, how the relationships with the relatives who remain at home are to be cared for, and so on. In some cases these public servants are living under conditions which are not as attractive as would be the case in Canada, but as I go around to different countries and have a chance to see them at their work I am very much impressed by the spirit they show and by the splendid work they are doing.

Within the last few days I had a very fine compliment paid to them by a distinguished diplomat from another country who has been in very close touch with members of the Canadian service. He said that man for man the Canadian foreign service is the best in the world. Unfortunately I am afraid he did not include the minister in that comment; but still I pass on this remark because I think these men and women deserve the praise.
I am also very grateful for the assistance which has been given by the representatives from other countries in Canada. We have a large number of distinguished diplomats in the diplomatic corps here, and their relations with us have been excellent. They bring to us a knowledge of conditions around the world, not only in their own countries but in other countries in which they have served, and they are a great help to the department. I believe in every case-I hope in every case; certainly in all that I have known-they go back to their own countries or to an office in some other country as friends of Canada. These men and their families have quite a lot to do with the good name Canada has in world affairs. I meet them in different places, at the United Nations, at NATO; wherever I go I meet someone who has served in Canada, and invariably they speak well of the way in which they have been treated and they have a great liking for our country. It is a privilege for me to be able to pay this tribute to them today.
In opening my report this afternoon I think it might be worth while to outline some features of the world situation at the present time before going on to make some comments on Canada's activities in world affairs. Since the disastrous blowing up of the summit conference we have all been living in the shadows caused by that event. Hon. members will recall that for many months the whole of the western world, indeed the whole of the civilized world, had been expecting wonderful things of the summit conference. Here in Canada we had hoped that there would be not only one successful conference but a series of such conferences, with the result that at least some of the difficulties in world affairs would be overcome.
I am not today going into details as to the reason for the failure of the summit conference or for the subsequent walk-out of the eastern five from the disarmament committee of 10 nations; but the cold, hard fact is that today we are living in the shadows caused by these two break-downs. There has been a lot of rather nasty name

calling and there has been a lot of propaganda certainly not designed to create good will in the world.
I find it rather difficult to ascertain exactly where communist propaganda ends or begins as related to policies. I think perhaps the communist nations have used propaganda in a different sense from the way in which we use it. Their propaganda might go off in one direction while their actual policy might go off at right angles, and they see nothing inconsistent in that. The policy is what they are really working at, but the propaganda is designed to influence world opinion. On the western side we always think that the propaganda and the policy are exactly the same, and it is very difficult for us to understand that probably they do not mean just the same thing. I do hear reports that the communist propaganda may be complaining bitterly about something, yet at the same time they are saying quietly, "We will go right ahead and carry on our negotiations. Don't be upset about what is being said in public; we still want to negotiate".
In any event, there has been an increase in tension in the world and, of course, Canada stands to lose as much as any other nation by tension. We lie between the two main protagonists, and the more tension there is the more likelihood there is of our sovereignty being interfered with and our right to run our own country being in jeopardy.
So much for the dark side of the picture. I will point out the other side. No doubt I will be accused of being an optimist, but I do not think a foreign minister would be of much use if he were not all for optimism. If he went around with his head down and thinking that the world was coming to an end, then in my judgment he would do much better to take on another job. On the bright side of the picture the conference on nuclear testing, in which the United Kingdom, the United States and the Soviet are participating, is still continuing. I was reading a dispatch this morning from Geneva, and I think it was reporting on the 267th meeting of that conference. Mind you, throughout all this time there have been no nuclear tests, apart from the French test in the Sahara. It is now almost two years since there was a nuclear test by any one of these three powers.
Another fact which I think is hopeful is that nuclear war still makes absolutely no sense, and I do not think it makes sense in anybody's country or in any language. The situation is still that if there is a nuclear war, in all probability civilization will be destroyed. There are voices raised occasionally to the effect that oh, well, we could have nuclear war and we could clean up this
Supply-External Affairs country or that one; but there are not very many responsible people anywhere in the world today who are not admitting that a nuclear war would probably mean the end of civilization.
Another hopeful fact is that in all countries there is a great, deep human yearning for peace. Perhaps most significant of all is that the nuclear powers are highly sensitive to world opinion. If they were not, if they did not get upset when criticized, I think the world would be in a very bad state. But you will notice, Mr. Chairman, that each of these nuclear powers is very careful not to go too far in the way of upsetting world opinion. They want to be able to justify their actions. At the United Nations in New York they rush to the rostrum to defend their actions just as quickly as some of the smaller nations rush to the rostrum to criticize.
It may be that the fact of their sensitivity to world opinion will be the means of saving civilization. That, of course, can only be done through the United Nations, but I am hopeful that world opinion as expressed through the United Nations by countries such as Canada and all the other countries that feel this way will eventually bring about the result that something will be done about cutting down and getting rid of armaments and living in a sane way in this world, in which under present conditions no one is more than 24 hours away from anybody else in any part of the world.
I go on now to review Canada's activities in certain fields. I am not going to try to cover them all in my opening remarks. My parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Oxford, will be dealing with some of them, and I know that others will come up in the course of the discussion of the estimates. However, I should like to make a brief review of five or six different fields which are of great interest to Canada.
First of all there is the field of disarmament. Canada has had and continues to have a very heavy responsibility in the field of disarmament because of our membership on the 10-nation committee. Last fall I thought it was a wonderful thing for Canada to be a member of the 10-nation committee on disarmament, but now I am not quite so sure that it was such a wonderful thing. Certainly it involved and still involves a great many difficulties and quite a few heartaches, and at times one is inclined to think it would have been very nice to be No. 11, not quite on the 10-nation committee but in a position to criticize the other ten. I suppose I get that from being so long in the opposition. There is quite a lot to be said for being an opposition member unless you are in the opposition too long.

However, I repeat that Canada has had heavy responsibilities in the field of disarmament. They involve, not only the work of the committee itself but the five western members on the committee had the additional job of advising the three western heads of government on the question of disarmament in connection with the summit meeting. That meant quite a bit of work, and unfortunately the work was all lost when the summit meeting blew up. But it did involve a great responsibility, and I am confident that nobody in Canada or in any other part of the world will dispute that our country made a sincere and honest effort to get results in the disarmament negotiations. We will, of course, continue to do so . either in this committee, if its sittings are resumed, or if disarmament is considered in the disarmament commission of the United Nations. In whatever field is available, Canada will be doing her best to further the cause of disarmament.
I should like to trace briefly our main activities as a member of the 10-nation committee. In the first place, we pressed for an early meeting. There were some of the western countries that did not want to have the disarmament talks commence until after the summit meeting had been held. If that advice had been followed we can see now just how tragic the result would have been, because very probably there would not even have been a meeting of the disarmament committee. We believed it was essential that the committee should get to work as quickly as possible so that progress could have been made by the time the general assembly meets again this fall and also because of the urgency of the problem. Our wishes in this regard were fulfilled and, as hon. members know, the committee commenced its sittings in March.
We have been in the forefront throughout on that committee in insisting that the United Nations should be tied in just as closely as possible with the work of the committee. It was at Canada's urging that references to the United Nations appeared in the original western proposals, and we had a good deal to do with a representative of the United Nations being in Geneva while the talks were in progress. We also stressed the need for bringing forward the problem of disarming so far as nuclear weapons are concerned. Some of the countries thought that should be deferred until the third stage, that nothing effective could be done about nuclear weapons until a lot of other things had been agreed upon. We believed, and in this we agreed with France, that nuclear weapons were of the first importance, and that there should


be at least some moves made to reach agreement on cutting down or doing away with nuclear weapons in the first stage of the proceedings.
We tried to avoid being provocative in the meetings of the disarmament committee. From time to time that was difficult for the Canadian representative, because some pretty violent accusations were made by the eastern side and I guess there were some pretty violent accusations made by the western side as well. Human nature being what it is, this is the result that follows. When one side starts to abuse the other there is a great temptation not to just sit and take it. Our Canadian representatives are human beings, too, and I suppose fall into the same temptation; but we have done our best to avoid provocative attacks on the eastern side.
As you know, Mr. Chairman, we have urged that there should be a series of balanced concessions. Some of the countries on both sides, but more so on the eastern than the western, wanted first of all to reach a general agreement which in effect would say, "We are all going to disarm", and that would have been about what it would have amounted to. That would have been about the sum and substance of the agreement. If they could not get everything at once they were not going to make a move.
It seemed to us that that was not a practical way in which to go about getting actual results; and as I reported to the house some weeks ago we decided to try to urge that there be a system of balanced concessions thereby at least making a start. Then we hoped that once a start had been made, we could go on to further saw-off arrangements and finally attain an agreement which had some value. In that course we have had support in Canada. I have here an editorial from the Globe and Mail of June 28. It is quite comforting to the government on occasion to have a favourable editorial of this kind from the Globe and Mail. Referring to the statement I made in the house it said as follows:
-the constructive approach at Geneva would have been for both sides to accept "a process of negotiation of balanced concession''. Instead of seeking agreement on a plan for wholesale disarmament, the delegates should have been willing to make gradual progress, finding agreement in limited fields.
I should not be surprised if, in the final analysis when a disarmament agreement is reached, that objective will be gained by some such system as this of starting from the bottom and working up rather than trying to build from the top down.
When the 10-nation committee reconvened after the failure of the summit conference

the Russians had new proposals to place before it. They issued them on June 2. They said that these proposals had been in their pockets when they were at Paris but that, because there had been no opportunity to hand them across the table, the proposals were going to be submitted when the disarmament committee resumed on June 7.
These proposals went part of the way to meet suggestions which had been made by the western countries. They were issued with a great flourish of trumpets. All the ambassadors to Russia were called in, they were handed a copy of these proposals and there was great press publicity about them. Obviously they were designed for propaganda if for nothing else. In any event, we believed that they merited the most careful consideration. After careful study of the proposals we had suggestions to make as to what the reaction to the proposals should be.
I have here a summary of the Canadian reaction to these soviet proposals. Mind you, this summary is not complete because there are some things which have had to be left out as four other western nations were involved and also there is always the question of security. However, if the committee is willing, I should be glad to have these Canadian proposals printed as an appendix to today's Hansard, so that they can be studied.

speechtext:
Once there had been this breakdown at Geneva in the 10-member committee we thought the best course would be to refer the whole matter back to the disarmament commission of the United Nations. In the final analysis the United Nations has the responsibility for disarmament; that is where eventually any final disarmament agreement will have to be arrived at. It was our opinion that there should be a request made to call the disarmament commission as quickly as possible and that the whole situation should be discussed there. We took that position throughout and we still take that position.
Mr. Hammarskjold, the secretary general, said at first that the disarmament commission should not meet until the dust had settled, and by that he meant meeting perhaps about the middle of August. Our belief is that it would be advisable to have a meeting of that commission at some time next month, rather than waiting until a week or two before the general assembly meets in September, as this has been suggested by some of the other countries. Whether or not this course will be followed I cannot say, but we believe that is the wisest plan.
The 10-nation committee has only been adjourned, it is not dissolved. It may be that eventually it will go to work again. Strange things happen in the world these days and this may occur. We suggested in the letter which the Prime Minister sent to Premier Khrushchev in reply to his rather critical letter to Canada that the past should be forgotten and that the 10 nations should

resume their work in the disarmament committee. I do not know whether that will happen or not; but as I say the committee has not been dissolved and Canada is only too anxious to carry on with this work either in that committee, in the disarmament commission of the United Nations or in any other body which may be set up for the purpose.
Now a few words about Canada's activities in the commonwealth. As you know, Mr. Chairman, our own Prime Minister once again played a very prominent part in the commonwealth prime minister's meeting which was held a few weeks ago in London, just as he did in 1957. Canada has a very responsible position in the commonwealth; we should realize that fact very clearly. After all, we are the senior member of the commonwealth next to the United Kingdom. We have had some experience in world affairs and we are looked to for leadership. I do not mean taking over leadership from the United Kingdom or anything like that, but Canada has a very big responsibility in the commonwealth today. I believe that responsibility was shouldered in an admirable fashion by our Prime Minister at this last conference.
One of the very valuable proposals which came from that conference was the plan to set up a system of aid to the underdeveloped members of the commonwealth in Africa. The decision was to study the possibilities of co-operative action for assisting the economic development of the commonwealth countries in Africa as the first step toward a program possibly along the lines of the Colombo plan. Work is going on at the present time in all the countries of the commonwealth in order that some scheme of that type may be got underway.
A decision was also made to investigate the possibilities for increased exchanges between commonwealth countries of persons with specialized skills and experiences, particularly senior administrators. The aid to Africa plan has those two different features and progress is being made on both of them. I believe this may turn out to be one of the most beneficial plans that the commonwealth has ever undertaken.
That brings me to the fact that Canada has a very important part to play in helping not only the nations which have become independent and are now fully fledged members of the commonwealth, but also the nations which are about to gain their independence. At the present time most of these nations are on the continent of Africa.
Hon. members will appreciate from what has been happening in the Congo within the last few weeks what a vital continent Africa is in the world today. At the same time I think

we will all be very grateful that the manner in which the commonwealth has launched new nations in Africa has been such that these new nations have been able to stand on their own feet and make real progress. This I think is one of the greatest accomplishments of British statesmanship.
On October 1 Nigeria is to become independent. She is the largest country in Africa with a population of between thirty and thirty five million people, and I believe Nigeria will play a very large part in the commonwealth, in Africa and in the United Nations. We are very hopeful of the future of Nigeria. A few days ago I had the minister of information of Nigeria visiting here, and in another two weeks we expect to have the premier of the territory of northern Nigeria with several of his officials. I also hope to be able to visit Nigeria on the occasion of their independence on October 1.
The relations between our two countries are very close. We now have a commissioner in Lagos who will become high commissioner upon Nigeria attaining its independence-I point that out to the hon. member for Essex East-and I do not think there could be a better friendship existing today between Canada and this country which is so soon to become one of the leading members of the commonwealth.
In addition the commonwealth scholarship plan which was initiated by Canada in 1958 is now getting underway. Eventually Canada will have 250 students from other parts of the commonwealth studying at our universities. This year we have only 104. Of course, these are two-year scholarships and there will be another course beginning next year, so there will then be approximately 250 in Canada. The department issued a press release the other day containing a list of the countries from which these young men and women will come. There are 14 from India, 11 from the United Kingdom, 10 from the West Indies Federation, nine each from Australia and Pakistan, five each from Ceylon and Ghana, four each from New Zealand, South Africa and Kenya, three from the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland, Malta, Uganda and Singapore, two from Malaya, Nigeria, British Guiana, Mauritius and Tanganyika and one from Basutoland, Bermuda, British Honduras, Fiji, Somaliland, Swaziland and Sierra Leone.
Some question was raised by the hon. member for Assiniboia as to the number of these students who would be going to French speaking universities, and this morning I answered that there would be seven out of the 104. This is one of the problems. There are not a great number of French speaking 79951-0-397
Supply-External Affairs students across the commonwealth and some way will have to be found to meet the situation. I am not yet in a position to say just how it will be done. If we suggested, for example, that arrangements be made to bring students here from the French community, which is what the French call their commonwealth, we could run into difficulties with France. I am not sure. But I realize this situation, and we would certainly like to get more French speaking students into Canada. The French speaking universities have cooperated wonderfully in this scheme. All the students have been passed by committees from the different universities, including the French speaking universities. There has been the best co-operation one could possibly hope for from the universities and this is a problem we should do our best to solve.
I am not yet in a position to say how many Canadian students will be going to universities in other parts of the commonwealth, because the final arrangements have not yet been made, but to date we have offers from the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Hong Kong, Malaya and jointly from Kenya, Tanganyika, and Uganda. This commonwealth scholarship plan is, I think, a splendid one and it could have far-reaching effects both on the commonwealth itself and on world affairs.
There is one difficult problem facing the commonwealth, and I would appreciate suggestions with regard to it from members of the house or of the Senate. It is this: are the smaller colonies, for example Malta and Mauritius, to have the same status as such countries as Nigeria, India, Pakistan, Canada, the United Kingdom and countries of that sort? There are about 16 of the larger countries which obviously would become fully fledged members of the commonwealth and about 30 or 35 of the smaller countries. What is to be done about the smaller ones?

An example, though not to the same extent as Malta. Is there to be some different arrangement for them, or are they to come in as fully fledged nations of the commonwealth? This is a very difficult question. At the moment my own opinion would be that it would be unwise to have first and second class citizens of the commonwealth. That does not make much sense to a Canadian. Just what course will be followed is certainly not clear yet. This matter is being studied very carefully and I have no doubt that the genius of the commonwealth for working out practical solutions will be in evidence here, too, eventually. But at the moment this is a difficult question, and we

Supply-External Affairs should be grateful for any bright ideas that hon. members of the house may care to put forward.
Now a word about Canada's activities in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. One of the main questions now before NATO is the proposal to draw up a 10-year plan. The United States suggested it last December, and everybody agreed that it was a very fine idea. I do not think anybody knew just exactly how to go about it, but now we are all working on this problem. The secretary general, Mr. Spaak and his officials are trying to work out a 10-year plan. Canada is trying to work on a 10-year plan, too. We have only got to the fourth year as yet. This, too, is a difficult operation. The United States are working out a plan and I hope that at the December ministerial meeting a 10-year plan will be put forward which can be considered and recommended for final consideration at a meeting of the heads of government of the NATO countries.
We are still plagued by the question of consultation in NATO. As hon. members know, we have done our share of howling about the three big countries going off into a corner and making decisions. We thought that was bad, and still do. We have been on this disarmament committee of five nations, and now the other 10 NATO nations think we are just about as bad as the three were. In so far as disarmament is concerned, there is a temptation for the five to discuss matters and then report to the NATO council about all the things they are agreed on, but not on what they are arguing about. The NATO council finds out anyway, in the corridors, what the arguments have been. But Canada has been on the receiving end in so far as consultation in regard to disarmament is concerned.
It is obvious you cannot keep an alliance strong if you do not have adequate consultation, and we must remember that just as much as the United Kingdom, France and Western Germany. We must remember the fact that there must at all times be adequate consultation.
Of course, there are many questions facing NATO. I am not quite as sure this year as I was a year ago that the Leader of the Opposition was being unwisely pessimistic about NATO. There were a few problems which gave him some justification for being a bit gloomy about the prospects of NATO. However, the spirit of the organization is very good. For example, every member of this house who belongs to the NATO parliamentarians association would agree with me that there has been built up quite a good comradeship in NATO. In addition to there being some very nice trips to Paris and other

centres, I am sure there is an attraction in this association for the members who belong to it because of the work that can be done to help strengthen the organization. Just a few weeks ago we had a visit here by NATO youth from various countries in the alliance, and there again you have young men, some of whom are parliamentarians, meeting together and discussing problems in a way which will help to increase the strength of the alliance.
With regard to our activities in the United Nations I can only say that Canada is continuing to play an active part there. The parliamentary secretary will deal with the refugee problem, radiation, the problems of outer space and several other questions which have been under very active consideration. We are continuing to be greatly interested in the peace-keeping machinery of the United Nations. Canada already plays as big a part as any other nation in the peace-keeping arrangements of the United Nations and the government is continuing that policy. It may be that some provision will have to be made for further support for the United Nations in this field. Certainly our minds are not closed and we are very much in favour of doing everything that Canada can do that is practical to help strengthen the peacekeeping machinery of the United Nations.
The Prime Minister indicated this morning that we are willing to have our observers in Palestine go to the Congo if Mr. Hammar-skjold wishes that done. We are also willing to supply airlifts to the United Nations to help in that country. Some question was raised about our battalion which was earmarked for service under the United Nations subject to Canadian government approval. That is not a practical step to be taken at the moment. For example, we have received dispatches today about the reaction of Ghana to supplying forces in Nigeria. Ghana considers that the present difficulty in the Congo should be solved primarily through the efforts of the independent African states within the framework of the United Nations machinery. Intervention by powers from outside the African continent in the view of the government of Ghana is likely to increase rather than lessen tensions. However, it is our general policy to give whatever support is practical and will be effective to help strengthen United Nations peace-keeping machinery.
At the session of the United Nations this fall I presume one of the main subjects will be disarmament just as was the case last fall and we shall try to help focus world opinion on the vital and urgent necessity of relaxing tension. I cannot give the committee any further details about Canada's plans for the session. They are in the process of formation

at the present time and it is too early to indicate what stands we will be taking on other questions.
A word or two about Canada's activities vis-a-vis the United States. We have just returned from a very successful conference of the ministerial defence committee. Ministers and their officials at these conferences are able to discuss problems in an informal way. There is no big table with one group lined up on one side of the table and the other group opposite them, with briefs and so on. There is no formality of that sort. The participants are able to review situations in the world which are of interest to both countries and of course they are able to review such questions as defence, NATO, disarmament, defence production sharing and all the questions which are of interest to the two countries. These are reviewed in a most informal and helpful way. I do not believe it would be possible to bring about such frank exchanges of views in any other way. These meetings are particularly helpful.
The same is true of the Canada-United States interparliamentary group. I am not sure that I have the right name of that organization but I refer to the plan under which 24 Canadian senators and members meet with 24 United States senators and representatives. That informal committee is doing excellent work in improving relations between our two countries. Canadians are able to talk to United States public men on a basis that is understood by the Americans and vice versa. For example, the action of the United States in holding off the diversion of water in Chicago last year was brought about to quite a large extent, I think, because of the discussions that took place in that interparliamentary group.
I had the opportunity to visit on the floor of the United States senate about three months ago. Their attitude toward us is very significant and it is so often overlooked by Canadians. Senator Aiken who is the head of the American section of this interparliamentary group was my host. He is, of course, a wonderful person with great attributes of friendliness. Referring to Canada he said:
It is a country which is closer to us than any other country in the whole world.
There was great applause from the senators following that remark. Senator Mansfield of Montana speaking for the Democratic party referred to Canada as:
-a nation which is most close to us; it is close to us not only in a geographic sense, but more important, in the sense of a shared outlook, shared ideals, and one may say, even a shared destiny.
It is possible to conceive of points of differences between the foreign policies and the immediate interests of Canada and the United States; that is inevitable among independent and equal nations.
