It is inconceivable, however, that Canada and the United States will ever permit these differences to transcend the deeper intermingling of the fortunes of the two countries.
I know I speak for my colleagues. Mr. Minister,-
He was referring to me, although I was too bashful to get up and make any reply. I know that hon. members can hardly believe that but it is true. I continue:
-when I say that the senate of the United States nourishes only the warmest sentiments toward Canada and the Canadian people. We wish for nothing more than a continuing abatement of any differences which may exist and a continuing growth of cordiality and co-operation in all spheres of relations with our great neighbour to the north.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister a question. Is that the Senator Mansfield who is supporting the increase in base metal duties to be imposed against Canadian imports?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
It may be, I am not sure. He comes from a zinc and lead producing state. He is entitled to have opinions about that just as we are entitled to have a few ideas of our own about zinc and lead on our side of the line. Senator Mansfield expressly stated that we would have differences and, as the Leader of the Opposition knows, we have differences and are going to have a lot more in the future, but we are able to sit down and talk about them and in most cases to work out some solution.
Finally, a word about activities in Latin America. There have been several visits between representatives of Canada and Latin American countries. The foreign minister of Venezuela was here last fall. The president of Mexico visited Canada and our Prime Minister returned the visit to Mexico a few weeks ago. The foreign minister of Brazil has also been here. Hon. members know that I visited Buenos Aires on the occasion of the 150th anniversary of Argentina in May. I also visited Chile and Peru with brief stopovers in Brazil and Mexico. Within a few weeks a Canadian minister will lead a delegation to attend ceremonies marking the 150th anniversary of the independence of Mexico.
We have invited President Frondizi of Argentina to visit Canada after the first of the year, and these visits are building up a great deal of good will.
The visit to Chile was particularly helpful because it came at a time when they were suffering the great tragedy of their earthquake, which was followed by floods and all sorts of troubles. The house was very good in supporting the action of the government with regard to that disaster and I think hon. members might be interested in two of the messages which have come back to us showing the reaction of the Chilean government

Supply-External Affairs and of the Chilean people to this aid given by Canada. I hold in my hand a message to the Prime Minister from the president of Chile, dated June 17, which reads:
It was the deepest sense of gratitude that I felt on reading the kind note which the ambassador of Canada in Santiago handed to me personally, and in which you reiterate the expressions of sympathy felt by the Canadian people and government for us, in the hour of these disasters caused by the series of earthquakes that have ravaged numerous provinces.
You further confirm in your letter information given me previously concerning the government's intention to send a large shipment of flour and canned meat so as to help in our relief work,- work that in view of the magnitude of the damage caused throughout the devastated areas, means every resource and effort must be strained to the utmost.
It is a duty incumbent upon me to express to you, Mr. Prime Minister, the profound gratitude felt by the government and by all Chileans because Canada's attitude towards us has been extremely noble in these, our tragic times. We shall always think of the help which you are sending us as an expression of closest solidarity with us and as evidence of the profoundly humanitarian sentiments of the great Canadian people.
I avail myself of this opportunity to tender my warmest personal regards as ever,
Jorge Alessandri R.
A very interesting report showing the reaction of the Chilean people came from the Canadian Red Cross representative in Santiago. He said:
The total Canadian effort is being recognized here in a very big way. We talked to people last night who had just come from a movie where R.C.A.F. planes, Canadian Red Cross disaster relief supplies, and Canadian personnel were shown. They said the whole theatre audience stood up and applauded for over five minutes at the sight, right through other news items.
I am sure that the hearts of Canadians will be warmed by that appreciation which was shown by these very courageous people of Chile in the face of their disaster.
As I told the house upon my return, we are setting up a Latin-American division in the department. We plan to have an observer at the conference of the organization of American states to be held in Quito, Ecuador, next winter and I am very hopeful that it will be possible in the near future to open a Canadian embassy in one of the Central American nations. We have no embassy in any one of those six nations at the present time. We have one trade commissioner in Guatemala, but I think there is a blind spot in Canada's diplomatic service and I am very hopeful that it will be possible to establish at least one embassy in Central America. We have embassies in all of the South American countries except Ecuador, Bolivia and Paraguay but we have none whatever in Central America.
Those Latin-American nations are developing very rapidly. They are going to be very big and strong before very long. There will be many millions more people south of the Rio Grande by 2000 A.D. than north of that river. All the nations there are very anxious to work more closely with Canada and I suggest that Canada would be wise to develop a western hemisphere outlook to a much greater extent than we have such an outlook at the present time. We do not seem to be able to see very far beyond the United States. For many Canadians the western hemisphere consists of Canada and the United States, and we just do not seem to realize that there are millions and millions of people beyond the Rio Grande who are playing a very important role in world affairs and who are extremely anxious to have closer relations with Canada.
Many western hemisphere problems involve us. We happen to live in the western hemisphere and we cannot get away from the effect of many of the events which take place on this side of the Atlantic. I suggest it is about time that Canadians realized that fact.
I had intended to mention the Pacific. However, I will defer my remarks on that and also on the law of the sea. I can deal with that later on when the estimates are open for question and answer.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, may I simply point out that Canada can play and is playing now a tremendous part in world affairs and can play an even greater part. We have the capacity to do that and we have the standing in the world to do it. For this I give credit to my predecessors who have been in this portfolio; they have all done great work. Canada has the capacity and she has the standing, and she can play an even greater part in world affairs. I do not put it forward as a challenge. I used to put it that way, but I put it forward rather as a responsibility. I believe we owe it to the world to play this great part that can be played by our nation, and in that suggestion I am sure I will be supported by every party in the house and by every hon. member. After all, it is something to be a citizen of a great country which is in a position to accept such responsibilities. My belief is that Canada in the years ahead can have a very large part in bringing the world back to reason and to co-operation and in so doing can attain the destiny which all of us have believed should be the destiny of our nation.
I thank hon. members very much for giving me extra time to make this review.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
First of all, I should like to say it is regrettable that the management of our affairs at this time of the session has been such as to render it necessary for committees of this house to be sitting while this important debate is under way. I as a member of the committee dealing with the bill of rights, because of a higher obligation at this moment in this house, have denied myself the opportunity of attending to my duties in that committee. I merely mention this; I am sure it represents some of the frustration that attends many hon. members in the house at this time.
To the Secretary of State for External Affairs I should like to say that I am sure we all appreciate his sincerity and his devotion to duty. We appreciate very much, particularly those of us on this side, the references made to his predecessors, than whom, of course, there was none more distinguished than the Leader of the Opposition.
As the Secretary of State for External Affairs said, the gap of differences in foreign affairs between the political parties in this house is certainly not as great as the gap of differences that exists in the matter of domestic problems. I think that generally we in this house agree on the basic principles of Canadian foreign policy. This, however, does not mean that we in this party are in accord with every phase of the government's policy, nor does it mean that we are precluded, because of agreement on basic principles, from expressing our differences and pointing out, as I shall endeavour to do today, what I believe are some inconsistencies in the foreign policy of the government of Canada at the present time.
When the minister spoke in the house on February 10 last he spoke, as he himself noted a moment ago, with an air of optimism. He had a confidence about him that in turn gave us confidence and that suggested that he saw some of the major problems of the day as not incapable of solution. Indeed he thought some of them were not incapable of ready solution, and among these was the problem of disarmament.
But since that speech on February 10 great deteriorations in international affairs have taken place. I refer to the failure of the four great powers to meet at the summit, as a result of the intransigent position taken by Chairman Khrushchev and the break-down of the 10-power disarmament meetings. The atomic powers are still in session on the question of cessation of nuclear tests, nevertheless the optimism the hon. gentleman had in February as to the likelihood of agreement
Supply-External Affairs between the three nuclear powers has certainly been marred by subsequent events. The good thing about those discussions, apart from agreements already entered into prior to February, is that they are still in session but the possibilities of settlement on the final points in issue are not too clear at this moment.
And so the minister began his tour d'hori-zon today with the background of these three situations confronting him and, indeed, if he had wanted to draw a more complete picture he could have pointed to other events in the world which are causing great concern at this time in the hearts and minds of civilized men and of their governments. The events in the Congo; the disturbing events in at least one section of Latin America, Cuba, involving as the situation there does very serious directions in Cuban-American relations, with their implications and their effects for other countries in the Americas, including Canada; the truculent attitude of the Soviet union during these latter days as evidenced by speeches involving threats of the use of force; all these situations present now a picture which I believe should cause all of us the greatest concern. I am sure they do cause concern to the minister just as much as to every other person who appraises the situation.
The great regret-I think that more and more now we may have to be prepared to affirm this-is that there seems to be lacking in the western world-I am not saying in every instance-the kind of direction from particular countries that we must look for if we are going to find a way out of the problems into which we, along with other nations of the world, have been plunged. Whatever may have been the situation in the past, I believe that no country today, regardless of its size, regardless of its importance, should shun its responsibility in asserting its position constructively and with responsibility regarding the great moving events now touching all peoples and all nations.
I believe that Canada has a particular responsibility now, perhaps more so than at any time in our history, to take the lead unhesitatingly in these matters where a lead is not or may not be taken on the part of great or smaller nations, particularly the former. There is no reason why we should not be prepared to embark on a carefully conceived and responsible foreign policy which would permit us to take initiatives toward this end. In the past, we have taken initiatives and have ventured into areas where before Canadian tradition would have denied us the opportunity. I do not say this because he sits on my left and is my leader, but the

Supply-External Affairs fact is that when the Leader of the Opposition occupied the post of secretary of state for external affairs he daringly did not hesitate to give leadership in great events not only in this country but to other nations of the world. It seems to me that the time is now more opportune than ever for that kind of responsible venture, daring and initiative. It seems to me it is with all this in the background that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has now got to look upon his heavy obligations as affording increasing opportunities, for constructive action, even though that may impose on him and on the government concerns that normally would not have attended a country like Canada.
The minister has dealt with a number of matters. I do not propose to deal with every situation he has covered. With a lot of the things he has said I am in full accord. He said, of course, that while he was an optimist in February he was not without optimism today but, to paraphrase his words, he did not now want to be regarded as a prophet of gloom. In the face of the situation that confronts us, I suggest that perhaps realism demands that we occupy a position somewhere midway between the optimism of the hon. gentleman in February and what he reluctantly refers to at the present time as moved of gloom.
I suppose we will not find it difficult to agree with the minister that he was right in part in February when he suggested that the situation in the world warranted us taking an independent position. I should think he regrets having taken the strong position he did at that time when he repudiated our former role of honest broker. I suggested to him at the time that we could still be an honest broker and provide our services in conciliation and mediation when opportunities presented themselves and without failing to look at matters through our own eyes and in the light of our own interests. Indeed I think on that occasion I said to the minister that while we had served in some particulars as a linchpin we had given a valuable demonstration of our desire to look at things in the light of Canadian eyes, particularly during the 10 years immediately preceding the advent of the present government into office.
I agree with the minister that for Canada one of the most important areas for constructive effort is in the field of disarmament. The minister was sanguine or overly optimistic I thought in February and earlier with regard to the possibilities, in spite of the failure to arrive at a settlement of major political problems of the world, when he discussed disarmament. The minister's enthusiasm was perhaps best reflected in the words which

he uttered some months after taking office when, in speaking of our opportunity in Canada, he said this:
Canada is growing in stature by the hour as a world power .. . Canada can play a vital part in world affairs today, perhaps just as vital as any other nation in the world. I believe we can make a greater contribution to world affairs than any other country in the next ten years. Above all Canada is a nation with an idealistic, unselfish approach ... Add Canada's good record generally . .. and the courage, common sense and God-fearing character of her people, and you will agree with me that we can give leadership in the finest sense of the word.
That is exactly what we want now. We want leadership. However, I would have expressed our opportunity in different words. The minister is not a boastful man, but it seems to me that in the statement I have quoted, there was a use of words not really characteristic of him. They have too much of the bravado in them, and they were words that possibly could best be left to others.
In terms of the role we can play I would prefer to rely on the assessment made of our foreign policies, of our governments, of our public officials, in the words of Mr. Kenneth Younger, a former minister of state for foreign affairs in Britain and now director general in the royal institute of international affairs who recently-as a matter of fact, it was early this month-in speaking of Canada's former role in foreign affairs said this:
Canada is a less important power in most ways than we are, but by sheer consistency in her support for the use of United Nations machinery, for new techniques of international conciliation and for collective organizations of various kinds, including NATO, Canada came to have an influence in Washington, in London and on the continent of Europe, which was disproportionate to her national power.
It seems to me that gives us an opportunity of playing a role of leadership in this setting -at the United Nations, at NATO, in the commonwealth, and in the context of the tur-bulency of our modern world-greater perhaps than at any other time. The minister has that opportunity, and I suggest to him that he has that responsibility.
The government must be clear in its own mind as to the course it wishes to pursue. The government has said that it is in favour of disarmament. I believe that is a proper objective, notwithstanding the fact that there are many voices in great countries today, who regard this as a dangerous pursuit in the light of the present international situation.
Only a few days ago I was reading an article which I have here and which was written by Mr. Chester Bowles. I mention him because of his growing importance in this field in the United States and because of political events now current there. He expresses

the view that the Soviet union does not really want disarmament, that we must assume that to be the case and, having made that assumption, that the United States must take certain positions that are certainly not fully consistent with the stated objective of the government of Canada.
Then of course there are other strong expressions of opinion along this line. We have recently read or heard of the report prepared by the so-called Gaither committee and the Rockefeller brothers, a report which produced, according to Mr. Bowles, a persuasive case for an immediate strengthening of the United States military position in which emphasis is given to the need for extended ground forces capable of fighting localized wars in any part of the world.
Those are important observations. They must be carefully considered by the government in the light of the stated objective that it has presented. Of course the minister qualifies this objective, as do we all, by stating that at this time we are not talking about unilateral disarmament, but we are talking about disarmament on conditions and under circumstances that will not prejudice our unity, the unity of the western world, the unity of the United Kingdom, of the United States and Canada nor are we talking about a disarmament that will in any way prejudice our security. We are all agreed on the necessity of the proper safeguards being observed, in order to see that all the terms of a disarmament agreement are maintained and adhered to by all sides. However, the government will have to assess carefully the position that some people in the United States take. Then it will have to determine if it is prepared, without destroying unity essential for the preservation of the free world, to take strong independent positions to promote the cause of disarmament within conditions which recognize interests of security and the unity of like minded states.
However, in order to do that, as I say, the government must know where it is going. The government must not only have a proposal in mind, it must not only be prepared to accept proposals or parts of proposals put forward by other countries, but there must be full agreement within the ministry on those matters that are of such vital concern.
Let me give an example, Mr. Chairman, of what I have in mind. The minister has said that the government is in favour of the cessation of nuclear tests. When questioned on the point, he said that the government was in favour of such a cessation with or without control; and the minister took pains in the committee on external affairs to repeat
Supply-External Affairs this position. He has never equivocated on this point. However, as he was reminded, or the Prime Minister was reminded on the orders of the day on June 6 last, that there was some equivocation in the government's position as stated by the Prime Minister himself. The Prime Minister went to Washington during Easter week. There he conferred with the President of the United States. Following these conversations a communique was issued. Among other things the following sentence appears in that communique;
Particular attention was paid to the importance of achieving with effective international control, an end to nuclear testing and progress towards general disarmament.
The words to which I draw the committee's attention are "with effective international control". That is not the stated position of the government.

I remember because the Leader of the Opposition and I had asked questions. The record is in Hansard and I looked at it again this morning. I asked the minister to look at this communique, to read its words and to see if any other possible interpretation was open other than that the Prime Minister was publicly on record as agreeing with the president that particular attention was to be paid to the importance of achieving the end of nuclear testing with effective international controls.
The United States does not support the position at the present time, that those tests which would take place under the ground can safely be left, until such time as scientific detecting machinery becomes available, to a mere agreement not to carry on tests. That is the position taken by the government of the United States. That is not the position of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but in this communique that is the stated position of the Prime Minister.

speechtext: The minister and I can spend much time on this and perhaps during the course of the estimates there will be an opportunity for further elucidation. But what I am saying, so that there is no misunderstanding, is that there is no doubt about the position of the hon. gentleman. There is no doubt about his having stated, without difficulty in comprehension, what he believed the position of the government of Canada to be. All I am saying is that the Prime Minister joined with the President of the United States in a statement which suggested that there could be progress toward the cessation of nuclear testing and general disarmament, with effective international controls. The Secretary of State for External Affairs said that the policy of this government was the cessation of nuclear tests with or without controls.

I am reading from the communique which will be found at page 4594 of Hansard for June 6.
We are, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs said, now a member of the 10-power disarmament committee just as we were a member of the former subcommittee. The minister will remember that in February, on the basis of what the United Kingdom had done at the United Nations and what the Soviet union had done too in outlining proposals for disarmament, we asked him what were the proposals of the Canadian government. The Secretary of State for External Affairs suggested to me during the course of the request which I made that I should appreciate that because of the delicacy of the negotiations, it would be unwise to publicize at that stage any proposal which the Canadian government had in mind.


I took issue with that particularly because, as I pointed out, Mr. Selwyn Lloyd, the foreign minister in the United Kingdom, had unhesitatingly stated in detailed form early in September the proposals which his government was prepared to advance as a means of bringing about a program of disarmament within the context of a system of controls.
However, when the Prime Minister spoke in the same debate on February 10 he did not seem fully to agree with the Secretary of State for External Affairs because he did outline what he regarded as the proposals which the Canadian government would present to the 10-power disarmament committee. Some of these proposals were outlined in a statement issued by the information division of the Department of External Affairs of February 11. First of all the Prime Minister said, among other things, in the third paragraph:
I suggest that immediate consideration and priority might be given to the control of missiles designed to deliver nuclear weapons of mass destruction and also to bring about an agreement as to whereby the location of missile sites should be designated.
I am not aware that there was any proposal put forward by Canada embodying this concept. I am aware that the French government, through Mr. Moch, did propose that there should be an agreement with regard to the means of delivery of nuclear instruments, and that Canada gave support to the French plan; but there is no Canadian proposal along the lines mentioned by the Prime Minister of which I am aware.
Then the Prime Minister made this further proposal, and all of these are, I think, depending upon their relationship and priority, important measures which must be achieved. I am talking about them in terms of a proposal and the extent to which we have taken an initiative, the extent to which we have asserted a position of responsible independence. The Prime Minister said in the fourth paragraph:
I believe the time has come that the nations should agree that the manufacture and use of biological and chemical weapons should be banned.
That of course is an objective with which we all agree, but I am not aware that there was any proposal put forward by the government of Canada embodying that objective. Then the Prime Minister went on:
.. .we come to the problem which transcends all these problems, namely that of outer space. 1 believe that outer space should now, before further advances are made in its exploration, be declared banned to other than peaceful purposes and that the mounting of armaments on satellites should be outlawed.

I am not aware that there is any proposal before the disarmament commission put forward by Canada which embodies that recommendation. Then the Prime Minister further said:
I would think that a major course leading to disarmament would be a declaration that the production of fissile material for weapons should be ended and that existing stocks should be transferred to peaceful uses as soon as a practical plan can be agreed upon.

I am not aware that that concept was put forward by General Burns on behalf of Canada at the 10-power committee meetings.
I do not have access to the verbatim proceedings of the 10-power committee, and I could be wrong. But I do share with the minister the desirability of making some progress in this very difficult field, a field where at least two nations have at their disposal instruments which, as he said, are capable of destroying even civilization itself. I share fully the minister's concern, and it is only because I do, that I am searching, through the means of this debate, for answers to some of my concerns.
What proposal did we make at Geneva? The minister said in February that we had a proposal but he did not feel it should be disclosed. So far as I can find out, the boldest step we took at Geneva was to make a statement, through General Burns, containing two passages of a speech made by the hon. gentleman in which there was a proposal for balanced concessions. Then there was a reference in the speech of General Burns to a stage by stage process. I suggest that an examination of the words of General Burns will reveal that there was no proposal put forward by Canada at all. What was done was to express, if I may use this phrase, a belief in a particular methodology, in a particular procedure that might or should be pursued at the Geneva discussions in order to bring about disarmament. Here is what General Burns said as reported in the Hamilton Spectator of July 6. He is reported to have said, inter alia:
He added this quotation from Mr. Green: "For example, the west might offer to negotiate a controlled limitation on force levels and related conventional armaments if the U.S.S.R. side would agree to negotiate on the nuclear disarmament 79951-0-398
Supply-External Affairs measures in stages one and two of the western plan ... if package deals of that kind could be made in several instances, the first thing we would know there would be a worth while disarmament agreement."
General Burns went on to suggest possible common ground between east and west on prohibition of placing weapons of mass destruction in outer space, a joint study of the cessation of production and destruction of stockpiles of nuclear weapons, and measures to set up international machinery to keep the peace in a disarmed world.
These are desirable procedural recommendations but they do not involve proposals to which could be attached these suggestions of procedure. Proposals were put forward by Great Britain in September, 1959. Proposals were put forward by the Soviet union on two occasions, one before the summit meeting and one immediately prior to the break-up of the 10-power talks. The United States put forward a proposal-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: I would point out to the hon. member that the proposals put forward were western proposals. It was not a United States proposal, but a western proposal in the making of which Canada had a very large part.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: I fully agree, and I do not deny that for one moment. But there was, first, this Soviet union proposal. There was a proposal put forward by France. There was a proposal put forward by the United States. It is true that Canada supported the French proposal-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: I do not want to have any confusion here. There was a western proposal put forward by the whole five western nations. On certain features of that Canada felt as France did, but the proposals were western proposals. When the western proposal was worked out Canada was just as much responsible as the United States, or the United Kingdom.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I am not disagreeing with what the minister is saying. I am trying to emphasize that this western proposal was not a proposal put forward by Canada on her own initiative. The proposal put forward at the first meeting of the disarmament committee by Mr. Moch was put forward in the name of France. It was not supported by the United States, but it was supported by Canada. It was a French proposal. There is on the record as far as I can ascertain no proposal that stands in the name of Canada.
The minister may say that the proposals of the various powers were such as to embody all the ideas put forward by Canada, and that there was therefore no need to put forward a Canadian proposal. The point is that the minister did say on February 10

Supply-External Affairs that there was a Canadian proposal, and I had been looking forward to seeing that proposal. The reason I emphasize this question of a Canadian proposal is that it could be that because of the competition that prevails in this matter and the pre-eminent place in disarmament discussions of the great powers, a proposal put forward by a country such as Canada with its recognized disinterestedness, speaking as she does not only for herself but for so many other nations, so many other thousands or millions of people in the world, might conceivably, I do not know, have made some impression on even the Soviet union.

speechtext: Does the hon. member think there should have been five different proposals put forward by the five western nations in the 10-member disarmament committee?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Perhaps there should not have been, but why talk of our independent stand? Why talk of our special Canadian proposal?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Here again, the hon. member must be more careful about these statements. I did not say Canada was going to put forward any separate proposal in the 10-member committee. I did say that Canada had put forward her proposals in trying to work out a western case.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Let me remind the hon. minister of what the Prime Minister said to Mr. Khrushchev in the letter he sent to that gentleman on July 2:
The Canadian government has throughout advocated in the 10-nation committee a strong and independent stand in support of balanced concessions leading toward agreement.
I ask the hon. minister to read Hansard of February 5.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Here again I do not intend to have my statements twisted. I tabled as an appendix to Hansard a statement having to do with balanced concessions. That statement had been made by General Burns before the Prime Minister's letter was written to Premier Khrushchev.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not object to the minister intervening in my speech, because this is an important matter, but the hon. gentleman will recognize that he can do it only if I agree, because these are not points of order. However, I do not object. I simply want to point this out: it may be it was correct for us to support a particular proposal, or series of proposals, because of a desire to maintain unity among the western powers. That may be. But we were confronted by the minister with an assertion regarding this matter, that there was going to be an independant position taken by Canada. No longer


were we to pursue the course of an honest broker. The implication of that was that we would stand on our own against friend and foe, and declare our position on these mighty matters as our conscience dictated. I am suggesting to the minister that he should remember the words he used at the general assembly on September 24, 1959, when he said:
The middle-sized and smaller powers must have an opportunity of being heard, for disarmament is of the deepest concern to all mankind. In Canada's work on the committee, we shall at all times keep these considerations very much in mind.
Those were noble words, and I believe the minister believed them, and I am sure he believes them now. Neither I nor anyone in this committee questions the goodwill and sincerity of the minister, any more than anyone will question the goodwill and sincerity of any hon. member speaking in this committee on this most vital matter, which affects the peace and security of the world.
But these words, in order to be given effect by those in authority, must be followed by action where action is desirable and possible, and I suggest to the minister that when the disarmament talks broke down, as he himself said, he urged that the matter be referred to the disarmament commission forthwith. Canada and the United States took that position. They took it, incidentally, before the Soviet union took the position that the general question of disarmament should be discussed at the next general assembly.
Expressing my own personal view I hope there will not be a meeting of the disarmament committee until the general assembly meets. My reasons for saying that are those given by the Secretary General of the United Nations. He thought that since there was a delay in convoking the disarmament commission all that we would see in the disarmament commission at a meeting prior to the general assembly, would be a display of propaganda, and bad temper, by the Soviet union, not calculated in any way to bring about a satisfactory solution.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Is the hon. member quoting
from the stand taken by Mr. Hammarskjold?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
No, I was not
quoting. I was merely saying what Mr. Hammarskjold said. He said he did not think it was wise that there should be a meeting of the disarmament commission at this time.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
But the fact is that although Mr. Hammarskjold said there should be some delay he did not suggest that there should not be a meeting before the general assembly. In fact, I believe he said that he thought

there should be one some time in August. I think that is still Mr. Hammarskj old's belief.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
It may be that I am wrong in that particular but according to his words, as reported in the New York Times, Mr. Hammarskj old said he did not concur-he did not mention the United States by name-in the proposal that a meeting of the disarmament commission should be called now. The minister can deny this if he wishes but I saw reports only last Thursday to the effect that the Canadian government is still of the view that there should be a meeting of the disarmament commission without undue delay. This is perhaps not a point of great substance, but it has a bearing on what I am trying to indicate, in the thought I am seeking to develop at the present time with regard to the role that Canada should play at the assembly.
At the assembly we will not be speaking in a meeting of the 10-power committee; we will be speaking as one member of the United Nations. I should like to see Canada, because of the experience she has acquired in these matters in disarmament talks, right from the first days at Church House in 1946, take a lead with countries like Australia, New Zealand, India and countries of that kind to see if we cannot develop a program of disarmament which could possibly have at least a persuasive effect, a certain psychological effect, in the world and which would be viewed I am sure sympathetically by western nations and I would hope by the Soviet union. What is to be lost by taking this kind of initiative? It may be there is no hope for disarmament until the question of Berlin is solved. The suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition in his carefully considered article in Foreign Affairs for June may be true. Perhaps it would be very difficult in the face of the opposition which the Soviet union takes with regard to its ideological interests to reach agreement on disarmament. The suggestion may be valid that the Soviet union might be unwilling to disarm at the present time because it does not satisfy her own interests or those particularly of her ideological partner, the Chinese people's republic.
Indeed, Mr. Chester Bowles says there is no hope for disarmament in the foreseeable future. He gives as his reason a genuine fear among the Soviet leaders of the very large forces which they themselves have brought into being; that their land-hungry Chinese neighbours would not permit it; that the Soviet union itself is the victim of its own tradition of secrecy; and that there are also differences in policy in the communist party 79951-0-398|
Supply-External Affairs which make any agreement on disarmament impossible on their part. That may be. Those who desire this-and among these is preeminently the minister-can only try, within the conditions of security to which I have referred, to see if they cannot do something about disarmament.
When the last proposal was put forward at the disarmament committee the minister replying to a question I put to him and to one which was put earlier by the Leader of the Opposition in the month of June-and I have the exact quotation with the four words he used-spoke of the soviet proposal as a definite step forward. Was it a definite step forward? That was not the position taken by the United States. The minister said a moment ago that Canada did not bring forward any individual proposal. Canada's name was attached to certain proposals put forward by the western powers. Did Canada support the last proposal of the United States? We have never been told that.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: If I may interject, Mr. Chairman, I pointed out to the house at the time of the break-up of the committee meeting that the United States had tabled their own proposal and that it was almost identical to the Canadian proposal, copies of which will appear in Hansard tomorrow.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: The minister says that the United States proposal is almost identical to the Canadian proposal. I have the United States proposal here, as it appeared in the New York Times and I have read it carefully.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I suggest that the New York Times is not a bible yet, and that it is quite often inaccurate.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I agree, Mr. Chairman, the New York Times is not necessarily authentic in all these things, but the minister will know that when it prints the texts of positions taken by countries they are generally regarded as reliable. I am handicapped, of course, because as the minister knows we do not have access to all the documents. I say that on the basis of the United States proposal, put forward on the Friday before the 10-power meeting ended, there is no great similarity or certainly there is not a detailed similarity between those general ideas which the minister calls the Canadian proposal and the proposal put forward by the United States.
The minister said the soviet proposal was a definite step forward. The very statement made by Mr. Eaton in the presentation of the United States proposal was an indictment of the soviet proposal. He referred to it as a plan designed to divide France from the other

Supply-External Affairs western powers. The minister must surely realize that these statements were made and that they call for clarification. I am not saying that my submission is fully substantiated. I can speak only on the basis of the material available to hon. members on this side of the house. I refer to the text of the statement of the United States proposal as given verbatim in the New York Times and I will be happy to see where that statement differs from the original text when that is made available.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. member appears to be referring to a speech made by Mr. Eaton-

speechtext: No, no.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: I was referring to the United States plan-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I was referring to that, too. I was referring to the plan made by the United States government, a plan the terms of which from article 1 to article 11 are given textually in the New York Times, and alongside that text is the verbatim statement of Mr. Eaton in the 10-power committee when he said, as I have just noted, that the soviet plan, which the minister said was a definite step forward, was a plan designed to divide France from the other western powers, and I suppose perforce that if Canada supported the French plan-and I think it was a wise action that the Canadian government took because the French government was seeking to deal with first things first- nevertheless in the commentary that Mr. Eaton made in reference to France, Canada also was therefore included.
Was there any discussion about the place of China in this matter? As Mr. Herter said, there is no question involving the recognition of communist China. But, as the secretary of state in the United States said, ultimately at some point, if there is going to be an agreement, that country has got to be brought in at some point if we are ever to have an agreement on disarmament. I do not know what the Canadian government's view is now but I note that the minister, speaking in Woodstock on March 16, as reported in the Globe and Mail, said:
But, he added, ultimately the Chinese position would have to be taken into consideration if total disarmament is to be achieved. Total disarmament must include China.
I would hope that when he speaks again the minister will have more to say about this particular situation. I know the minister will not mind my emphasizing that the situation today is different from what it was in February when he was so optimistic. I have before me the Montreal Gazette of April 8 in which I find the following:


External affairs minister Green said today that an agreement on cessation of nuclear tests among the United States, Russia, Britain and France is "imminent".
We know today that whatever may have been the situation then it is not imminent now. While Canada is not a member of the three-power nuclear talks, because of the relationship of the cessation of tests to a disarmament treaty the Canadian government owes to this committee and to the people some indication of what brought about this deterioration. Was it because of the position that the Soviet union took prior to the abortive meeting. Was it because of hesitancy at first and the later position taken by the government of the United States? If this is so, were consultations held between Canada and the United States toward bringing about some agreement on the cessation of tests? These and other questions are, I am sure, of concern to the minister and to the people of this country. We ought to be given whatever answers can be given without in any way interfering in the negotiations which we recognize must be carried on sometimes in private in order to bring about results which then must become public.
I believe that in Canada we have a great responsibility. I can understand how the minister feels now about the situation, in terms of our membership on the 10-power committee, but we have a responsibility as a member of the United Nations; we have a responsibility as one nation in this dangerous, turbulent world of ours. Because we do deserve the praise that is levelled at our public service, and the tradition of our foreign service in particular and because of the minister himself and of his predecessors, we do have an opportunity which I believe we are not exercising to the full.
The minister is an able man. The minister, as I said, is a sincere man. He believes in the desirability of controlled disarmament. I suggest to him that if he will develop that sense which we all know he possesses and if he will take initiatives of a responsible kind he will find that those initiatives may have results. I hope that the phrase "easing of tensions" is not too pretentious, but he might be able to bring about positive and constructive results from the efforts that I suggest he make.
The minister has just come back from South America. He made a tour of some nine days, visiting several countries there.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I am an expert now on South
America.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not think
the minister would be an expert, but I know he is a more knowledgeable man and certainly

better equipped to deal with certain problems than before his visit. He told us in the committee on external affairs that at a time when United States-Cuban relations were so tense Canada enjoyed very close friendship with Cuba. The minister did not speak today of this situation. This is one of the current topics, one that affects us all in the Americas, one that could easily affect the balance of our position in the world vis-a-vis the Soviet union. What is the minister's view of the situation? Is there any accommodation that can be given by the government of Canada in this matter? Has any offer been made by the Canadian government with regard to this particular situation or does the minister feel that it is a dispute which Canada should keep out of? If that is the position, then certainly it is not consistent I believe with our obligations under the charter of the United Nations. I am not suggesting that the minister should plunge in headlong. He knows I am not making that suggestion. If our relations with Cuba are so cordial, is there not something that we can do or is there not something that we can try to do?
The Prime Minister went to Mexico. That was a successful visit. The Prime Minister was received warmly and, as Canadians, we were all proud that was so. The minister himself was received generously by the people of the countries in Latin America which he visited. The minister did say at one time that he was in favour of joining the organization of American states. Let me refer to the Vancouver Sun of June 17, in which the following appears:
External affairs minister Howard Green said Thursday night that Canada should join the organization of American states if its long term aim is to share in world leadership.
Then the minister is quoted as saying:
"Our objective right now is to increase our contacts with the Latin American nations as much as possible," Green said in an interview.
He denied that if deliberations now taking place in Ottawa decide in favour of Canadian membership, Canada will face obligations of aid to Latin American nations and defence commitments under the Rio pact.
"Any aid we supply goes through the United Nations," he said. "However, it is quite possible that this would be increased."
What is the position of the government? The minister told us of his visit but he did not tell us whether we were going to join the organization of American states. The minister owes it to the country to explain exactly what is in his mind, particularly in the face of the current situation in one close-by South American state.
Is it the policy of the government that we should join the organization of American
Supply-External Affairs states? If that is the case, will the government give us the reasons for this view? This is an important matter. I suggest to the minister of external affairs that in the face of the alarming situation in the world-I do not want to add adjectives that seem to be excessive, but we must all recognize it as alarming-in the face of the situation in Asia and some developments that have taken place in Africa; in the face of the intransigence of the Soviet union and the development in Latin America, are we drifting into a situation where, because of the policies of certain countries that have done so much for mankind and for the world, which policies are practically misunderstood, there is now rising in so many areas of the world hostility toward the things that we stand for basically in the west. If that development is taking place, the man who can speak with certainty about our position is indeed a brave one. Into that kind of a situation the minister is plunged, and I suggest to him that in the position that he takes, during consideration of his estimates, he ought to give us a clear appreciation of how he conceives these developments and their effect on us in terms of their effect on the free world. He should tell us what this government thinks it can do in the exercise of its rights and duties as a member of the United Nations.
The minister spoke of the commonwealth, and with everything he said we fully agree. But because we are in the commonwealth, because we are a close neighbour of the United States, because of our friendship with some of the older members of the commonwealth, countries like India, Ceylon and Pakistan, and newer members like Ghana, we are in a position to exercise a sphere of influence for the good and the peace not only of Canada but of the world. Nothing short of an effort on the part of the government, clearly demonstrated in all its permissible details, can satisfy at this time.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when I view the beauties and glories of this land of ours, when I see happy children at play, when I witness young couples building homes together all across the country I, along with many others I am sure, am frightfully conscious of the fact that their fate rests in the hands of those people responsible for decisions in foreign affairs. Since we last had a debate on the minister's estimates there have been unfortunate developments and an unfortunate change in the atmosphere so far as international affairs are concerned owing to the U-2 incident, the collapse of the summit conference and, more recently, the collapse of the disarmament conference. I am sure we all regret these unfortunate developments,
6308	HOUSE OF
Supply-External Affairs and yet I agree with the minister that regardless of the disappointments we have still got to continue to work in good heart and spirit toward the goals we hope to achieve.
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, when dealing with international affairs no party in this house under the present circumstances should seek to gain political advantage by making unsound though what might appear at the time temporarily popular proposals on this question. I also believe that no individual should shrink from unpopularity through failure to tell the truth as he or she sees it on these important questions. The minister mentioned that with respect to foreign affairs we have a tripartisan policy in this country. I think it would be more correct to say that we have a tripartisan purpose in this country and in the house.
I listened with interest to the minister's report. I simply say, and I am sure in saying so I have the endorsement of all hon. members of the house regardless of party, that we hold the minister in the highest regard. As the hon. member for Essex East said, we recognize his sincerity, his devotion to duty and his industry, and we also recognize the capacity and industry of the very efficient staff of his department. Like the last speaker, on several occasions when I have been in New York, Washington, Paris or London I have heard favourable comments from representatives of other governments with respect to our Department of External Affairs, comments by people who come in contact with our officials to quite an extent in these other countries and who have learned to recognize their ability.
We in Canada have been fortunate with respect to this department. Without hesitation I pay tribute to the secretary of state for external affairs under the former government and, as all Canadians do, give him credit for the things he has done in the past. I think his major achievement was the work he did during the Suez crisis in bringing about a common approach on the part of various nations and finally a common approach between those that were on one side and on the other side of the question. Out of that work arose the idea of establishing a United Nations emergency force, an idea that at the time was scoffed at in some quarters, but we are very glad to know it is an idea that has borne fruit, which was very useful in the Suez incident and is going to be useful in the Congo situation to which reference has been made today. In that respect I simply want to say, with all the criticism of the United Nations and the disappointments, what would we do in the world at the present time in meeting
[Mr. Herridge.l

situations from day to day such as the one in the Congo if we did not have a United Nations emergency force?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: We would have to find another one right away.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
We would have to find some other type of organization or we would drift into unilateral action which would make the situation even worse. With respect to our present minister, I think we are very fortunate and I have in mind his interest and attention to his work and his very definite statements with respect to nuclear testing. The hon. member for Essex East twitted him somewhat about that but we in this group are very pleased that he has made definite statements and has said "period" at the end of each statement. We think that sort of definiteness is very necessary at this time.
We are also pleased with his interest in and serious concern for the problem of disarmament and also his particular interest in the strengthening of commonwealth ties and united action on the part of the commonwealth on these most serious questions. Finally, we are pleased with his moderation. Under present world circumstances I think we are very fortunate in having a Secretary of State for External Affairs who does not get panicky, who does not get the jitters but takes a moderate and calm approach to these questions. I presume that like the previous secretary of state for external affairs he has learned to be somewhat philosophical as a result of his war experiences. It does not do to become too excited on occasions if you want to survive.
In the limited time at my disposal I intend to launch into a subject dear to the minister's heart, namely disarmament I was very pleased to hear him say that he was proposing the reconvening of the disarmament committee and is making efforts to have the work continued that was unfortunately stopped by the withdrawal of the Soviet representatives from the disarmament committee talks. We were very pleased to hear his statement in that respect and we will support him in all he does.
But on behalf of our party, and I speak for the party on this question this afternoon, I want to deal with a more local aspect of disarmament over which we have control and with respect to which we may set some example to the rest of the world. This problem is causing increasing concern to people across Canada and there is increasing interest on their part because of their awareness of the frightful situation into which the

world could very easily drift through the mistakes of a very few individuals. This is indicated by editorials in newspapers, particularly in the Globe and Mail, a Conservative organ which sometimes criticizes the government with respect to foreign affairs, by church organizations, co-operative organizations, labour organizations, women's organizations and various other groups across the country.
In these proposals on behalf of the group I represent I wish to offer some constructive but definite alternatives to present government policy in this field. I am going to pay closer attention to my notes than I usually do because in dealing with a subject like this I think one must be careful not to phrase a sentence incorrectly. Therefore I trust the committee will bear with me. We think this is a positive approach to a problem over which we have direct control and on which we can demonstrate to the rest of the world that we are doing our little bit in that direction.
Most discussions on foreign affairs in our country start from the premise that Canada is closely bound to the foreign policies of the United States. The implication is that our interests are similar, and there is no doubt that they are similar in many respects. Independent action by Canada is unthinkable, particularly with respect to this premise. The adherents of this view claim that they are being realistic. The realists say: What about defence? You cannot ignore geography. We are placed squarely between the U.S.A. and the U.S.S.R. That is quite correct. Quite so; and in pre-nuclear times we would have been forced to accept the military status of outpost of the United States, a logical complement, besides, to our economic and political status of satellite. But we are now in an age where the outbreak of total war would lead to the utter devastation of North America. Therefore, in our opinion, the acceptance of the status of outpost implies acceptance of the notion of actually fighting a thermonuclear war or, in other words, of committing international suicide.
I am not saying that thermonuclear war is impossible. Lemmings are not the only creatures to act irrationally. What I am saying is that there is no sense in preparing for suicide, especially if such preparations, the major part of our defence activities, cost hundreds of millions of dollars annually and deflect us from doing anything worth while to lessen the ghastly possibiilty of thermonuclear war.
In his contribution to the foreign affairs debate in the house on February 11 last the Prime Minister suggested as point two of his
Supply-External Affairs disarmament plan-to which we listened with great interest-the following:
-immediate consideration and priority might be given to the control of missiles designed to deliver nuclear weapons of mass destruction and also to bring about an agreement whereby the location of missile sites should be designated.
Those words may be found at page 991 of Hansard. I read that proposal with great interest and I want to say this. The Prime Minister's suggestion seems to indicate that he is unaware that the defence strategies of the U.S.A. and the U.S.S.R. are based on deterrence. Far from "immediate consideration and priority" as he says being given to his point No. 2, this is from our point of view-and I am putting forward our point of view on this matter-practically the last step to be taken after the major powers have disarmed themselves of conventional weapons.
I just suggest this to you, Mr. Chairman. Imagine a situation in which the U.S.A. and the U.S.S.R., both fully armed, know the location of each other's missile sites. It may be assumed that they already know the location of each other's H-bomber airfields. I make this suggestion to you. Would not each mighty power feel an overpowering urge to strike at the other's missile sites and airdromes lest the other strike at his?
The balance of terror-that is deterrence- is stable only when neither, in striking first, can destroy the other's ability to strike back. If the locations of all missile sites and H-bomber bases were to be revealed now, the balance would become highly unstable, in our opinion, since with sufficient missiles each side could be sure by striking first of destroying the other's ability to strike back. Undoubtedly-and we recognize this-the Prime Minister was seeking to have the dangerous deterrent posture of the mighty powers evolve to one of peace. His suggestion, however, would in our opinion cause these powers to adopt a posture of extreme provocation.
Control over the thermonuclear deterrents of the U.S.A., the United Kingdom, and the U.S.S.R. cannot come until the final stage of total disarmament, immediately prior to the dismantlement of these deterrents. We put that forward as a possible new approach to this present situation.
In a letter to Mr. Khrushchev on January 18, 1958 the Prime Minister offered to open all or part of Canada to aerial and ground inspection on a basis of reciprocity. We must realize this when we deal with that proposal. There are no offensive intercontinental weapons in Canada, no H-bombers, no ICBM's. We may be sure there are some in the northern U.S.S.R. How could one expect
6310	HOUSE OF
Supply-External Affairs Mr. Khrushchev to accept the Prime Minister's offer under these circumstances? We put that forward as a question.
In our opinion we must get away from second world war ideas of air defence. There is no defence against thermonuclear weapons, and everyone knows it. From our point of view, NORAD is almost useless. You will recall, Mr. Chairman, that when the vote was taken in the house establishing NORAD this party opposed this unilateral action by the establishment of NORAD. For us to be a staunch ally of the U.S.A. in the third world war on this basis, from our point of view, is neither wise nor sensible. I want to emphasize the fact that we have not suddenly lost our friendship for the Americans. The point is that to prepare for suicide, for the third world war, is nonsense, from our point of view. Does a man prepare to celebrate his own wake or does a nation do so? Rather than thinking of ourselves as the northern outpost of the U.S.A., we must think of ourselves as the essential buffer, in the opinion of this group, between the U.S.A. and the U.S.S.R.
Since all parties recognize that a major war is international suicide,-and the minister himself has made that statement on a number of occasions and we agree with it- we must do all we can to prevent it. We Canadians can best prevent it, in the opinion of this group, by separating as much as we can the U.S.A.'s strategic air command from the U.S.S.R. and the Soviet long range air force from the U.S.A. In this we believe we serve peace and serve the best interests of the U.S.A. and of the Canadian people.
The D.E.W. line serves as a deterrent to thermonuclear war by its constant ability to alert SAC of the approach of soviet H-bombers. The U.S.S.R. will not send H-bombers against the U.S.A. knowing full well that SAC will be alerted in time to attack the Soviet union. I think that is a sound proposition or a sound way in which to analyse the matter.
But the balance of terror tends to be unstable. I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that by internationalizing the D.E.W. line, by giving the Russians the same assurance against United States attack as we at present give the United States against Russian attack, we lessen the necessity of both sides to think in terms of preemptive attack. Of course, this assurance will not be absolute. Bombers do not have to fly over the D.E.W. line and ICBM's and nuclear missile-firing submarines operate outside the scope of the D.E.W. line's radar. But internationalizing the D.E.W. line-that is, by permitting Russian radar technicians to sit side by side


with United States radar technicians-we believe would be a wise step forward.
It is a true step toward disarmament for it disarms, to a certain extent, the opposing strategic air forces. It is something we Canadians can do. It would be a much more worth-while proposal to bring to the disarmament conference than are some of the proposals made to date.
Finally, this proposal points the way to control of ICBM's: world-wide internationalized missile tracking radar scopes. If each side knows it cannot fire a missile toward the other without the other knowing of it within seconds, then we have eliminated fear of surprise ICBM attack and we have eliminated what will otherwise become the major cause of pre-emptive attack in the future.
In this connection we would recommend to the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs, as well as to all those engaged in disarmament negotiations, that they read the first rate article in the July issue of Foreign Affairs by the distinguished United States professor and author, Dr. Henry A. Kissinger, a very interesting article indeed. The article is called "Arms Control, Inspection and Surprise Attack" and commences on page 557 of this issue. If members of the government would read this article we would hope that our future disarmament negotiations might take more account of the realities of the present situation in this age.
It may well be that we will not have complete and general disarmament until we have true world government. We do not underestimate all the difficulties and the risks involved; anyone who did so would be foolish. Until then the least we must work for is an end to the nuclear arms race, disengagement as far as we can achieve it and disarmament in peripheral areas, and a scaling down of the thermonuclear deterrents of each major power to a level where they deter but do not provoke an attack by the other.
Disengagement in North America means, as I have explained, that Canada must leave NORAD. I agree that when Canada does some people in NATO will claim that we have gravely weakened the defences of the free world. We oppose NATO because we oppose the unilateral defence system. We believe in action through the United Nations by the United Nations organization.

speechtext:
I should have said I was opposed to NORAD and I correct myself. We

insist that NORAD adds little to our defence. The only intercontinental defence is deterrence and this is a function of the strategic air command, Polaris-firing submarines, missile cruisers, aircraft carriers and United States nuclear weapons based in Europe and Asia. We want to emphasize the fact that in all this Canada has no part whatever.
But we must not think that leaving NORAD means we can sit back and let the rest of the world go by. We see no virtue in isolationism. Indeed such an approach is repugnant to every true democratic socialist. Anyone who understands the socialist philosophy knows that you cannot isolate yourself from the rest of the world and become an isolationist if you are to accept your responsibilities. We know that we will have to operate the D.E.W. line and back it up with fighter aircraft capable of identifying and intercepting the most modern bombers. That is, we will still require armed forces in Canada sufficient to allow us to be a buffer. But we cannot do this on the cheap. For Canada to play an honourable role in world affairs we must spend what is necessary to provide this type of defence and increase our aid to underdeveloped countries in which we believe we should play an even greater part.
Now I turn to NATO and explain our position there. First, it is in Canada's interest that the nations of NATO not fall under communist domination. Second, the defence problems of the European members of NATO and Turkey are fundamentally different from those of the United States and Canada; the NATO area is contiguous to the U.S.S.R. and we are not. I believe it is in Canada's interest that NATO'S strategy reduce the dangers of war to the minimum consonant with the territorial and political integrity of the nations which comprise NATO. Regardless of why massive soviet forces are in eastern Europe, so long as they are there NATO must be powerfully supported by the western allies. However, the present military situation in Europe is that the NATO forces are greatly outnumbered by the Russians in effective combatant formations.
Western policy is to balance NATO's weakness in conventional forces by being ready to use so-called tactical nuclear weapons. This idea is based on two false premises: first that a weak force armed with nuclear weapons is going to beat the large force armed with nuclear weapons; second, that a nuclear war in Europe could possibly remain limited.
Canada must insist that NATO recast its strategy, its tactics and its organization so that its defensive forces are capable of meeting any soviet aggression with conventional weapons long enough to allow diplomacy to
Supply-External Affairs seek a settlement before, progressively, tactical nuclear weapons and thermonuclear weapons are used. We say that we should make it very clear to our NATO allies that we will withdraw from the alliance unless they all honestly strive to give effect to disarmament and disengagement. The whole idea is to work toward the creation of a buffer zone in Europe at the same time as we make a buffer zone of Canada. That is our approach to this problem at the present time.
We believe that the NATO powers must give the Rapacki plan the consideration it deserved in the beginning. From the beginning NATO has unfortunately been a purely military alliance, and so many cultural and economic organizations have grown up outside of NATO that it is useless now to think of NATO in any terms except military terms. We say that our membership in NATO must be contingent therefore on NATO fulfilling a useful defensive function, which we believe it can.
At first sight it may appear strange to advocate that Canada leave NORAD at home and yet support NATO abroad. The reason stems from what must be the basic aim of our defence policy, and that is to prevent war. The fact of the matter is simply that in the first place NORAD, from our point of view, is useless and, in the second place, by being a buffer in North America Canada can best prevent an all-out, pre-emptive war between the United States of America and the U.S.S.R.
On the other hand, were we simply to quit NORAD without making the slightest attempt to modify NATO's strategy and organization, we would not have done all we could to prevent world-wide war breaking out in Europe, a war in which we would surely suffer annihilation.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I have dealt with that situation as a contribution toward the study of the question of disarmament within a field over which we have control and in which we can make decisions, and as a contribution toward lessening world tension. We in this group are very keen on nuclear disarmament and we are very pleased with the statements the minister has made from time to time on this question. This is a matter of increasing concern to people across this country, as evidenced by resolutions passed by various organizations, churches, trade unions, co-operative societies across this country and so on.
A very interesting resolution was passed on this question by the fiftieth congress of the co-operative union of Canada last April. Another was passed by the United Church of Canada and unanimously passed at its council meeting.

Supply-External Affairs
Then I noticed recently that Commander Sir Stephen King Hall from Great Britain has taken a strong stand in the leadership of the movement to work for nuclear disarmament. In that connection I would like to draw the attention of the committee to a statement made by the Prime Minister in the house recently, when he said that he wanted to make it abundantly clear that nuclear weapons will not be used by Canadian forces except as the Canadian government decides and in a manner approved by the Canadian government, and that Canada would retain its full freedom of choice and decision. In view of the newspaper reports I received we would much like the minister to reconcile that statement with the reports we have been reading in the press in recent days when he replies at the end of this debate.
However, we do want to emphasize our support for all efforts to end nuclear testing and to promote nuclear disarmament. As the minister said this afternoon, nuclear war means the end of civilization so it is up to us to contain ourselves and do the best we can in the circumstances though they may be trying at times.
