speechtext:
I thank the committee, Mr. Chairman. I have only a brief further word. As I was saying it would be most regrettable if contributions to the splendid work done by the Canadian committee for world refugee year were discouraged as a result of misunderstandings such as this. I am quite sure that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam was misinformed. I have taken this opportunity to clear up the misunderstanding because it would be unfortunate if this false impression got abroad and further contributions to this worthy cause were thus subject to interference.
I believe it is fair to say that the contribution to world refugee year which has been made by the government and by the private campaign co-ordinated by the Canadian committee has been a substantial one. Although we have reached the end of world refugee year it is clear that this does not mean the end of Canadian support for programs of assistance to refugees. The Canadian committee will continue its campaign until September 30 and the national voluntary *organizations will continue their regular programs indefinitely. For its part, the government intends to continue its substantial contributions to the regular budgets of the United Nations refugee agencies and will continue to give sympathetic consideration to proposals designed to ass;st refugees.
That concludes the remarks I have to make on this subject. Again I wish to thank the committee for permitting me to complete my remarks.

maintopic: CANADIAN REACTION TO SOVIET DISARMAMENT PROPOSALS OF JUNE 2, 1960
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I ran across a rather interesting item in the New York Times magazine of February 9, 1959 which reads as follows:
At no time in history have nations been granted the privilege of defending themselves both successfully and also at a level they think they can "afford". There is no reason to suppose that history has obligingly reversed itself for the benefit of the west.
This paragraph, of course, refers to the tremendous financial cost of nuclear armaments and the equally high cost of nuclear defensive weapons. No one will disagree that

this is a rather striking statement. I think it is even more striking when we stop to consider that in spite of its astronomical cost, nuclear warfare because of its unprecedented destructive power is not and cannot be the accepted solution to the relatively minor international Conflicts between the nations who will resort to it. Of course, these conflicts and incidents such as we have read about recently will be the excuses given for launching into nuclear war but the true spark of nuclear war will be an absolutely insane pride and thirst for power on the part of one nation and the fear of losing face on the part of another. Of course, this would not be the first time in history that the world has been plunged into the horrors of war because of the ambition and pride of madmen, but precisely because it is not the first time and precisely because we do not want to repeat what has happened in the past we should not make the same mistake and suffer consequences which would be infinitely more disastrous than we have ever known.
If we are willing to pay prohibitive costs for the production of nuclear weapons knowing that a nuclear war is not the solution to international problems, surely we should not hesitate to do all we can to seek, find and accept truly imaginative, determined and even revolutionary foreign policies which might prove to be a more practicable approach to world peace and stability.
No one doubts, I am sure, the intellectual ability of man in finding true safeguards to world peace. This has already been done theoretically in the United Nations, but there is an evident though understandable lack of determination and a hesitation among the members of the United Nations in implementing these safeguards and in making them work.
I think we are all agreed that the United Nations is not only the best but is the only means devised to date of establishing healthy, intelligent and practicable international relationships. Although it has never been overpublicized, the United Nations has been particularly successful in bringing much-needed economic and social aid to many nations of the world and it has created better understanding among them in these particular fields. But it would be ridiculous to pretend that the security council and the general assembly have been able to come up with anything more than almost meaningless resolutions in the political field and it would be hazardous to pin all our hopes for settling of international disputes and maintaining world peace exclusively on this agency as it now operates.

Now more than ever before are we being challenged to find and to live up to international policies which can be the alternative to war and destruction and which can bring about the greatest amount of security and stability toward which each nation is striving and to which it has every right. One thing is evident, that we have not yet found that alternative and the world is being brought gradually closer to the brink of a disastrous war. It would appear that there is a very strong and stubborn tendency to attempt to fit old solutions to new circumstances rather than analysing current problems and accepting the solution suggested by the facts no matter how far removed from the traditional practices.
One notable exception to this tendency of applying old formulas to new situations is the revolutionary principle on which is based the European common market which has been found to be a practicable solution to Europe's economic problem but which ten years ago was considered impossible because it did not fit in with the accepted economic principles and the traditional theories of national sovereignty. It may well be that before we can hope to find the appropriate solution in international affairs we must be ready to analyse the real causes of world unrest and instability and be determined to accept the solution that would be most apt to bring about world peace, no matter how unorthodox it may at first appear.
A look at the world picture today is the best indication that an alternative is necessary and urgent and to ignore these warning signs would be a repetition of the years prior to the second world war when as an excuse for inaction we tried to convince ourselves that Hitler would not dare, and war in our generation was impossible. Well, he did, and it was.
There is, among other things, internal strife in the Congo, Italy, Japan, as well as in Algeria, South Africa; there are most disquiet-ening events between Cuba and the United States with several disconcerting asides between the United States and the U.S.S.R. The summit meeting was made to collapse and plunged the world again in the deep freeze period of the cold war. All our hopes of attaining some agreement on disarmament have been dashed to the ground and we are back again to where we were 15 years ago.
It would be very easy and indeed not unwarranted to rile the government and the Secretary of State for External Affairs for the unrealistic optimism displayed earlier this session with reference to the summit meeting and the disarmament committee. But without saying "I told you so" I think we can be
Supply-External Affairs permitted to point out that, unlike the government's optimism which was based on nothing more than bravado and wishful thinking, the foreboding of the opposition which was characterized by the government as doom and gloom was based on reality and on a thorough knowledge and realistic appraisal of the behaviour of the U.S.S.R. over the years. Subsequent events have confirmed our forebodings. It is not only folly, but it is dangerous for the government to continue its off the cuff foreign policy based on nothing more than wishful thinking and pious hopes apparently oblivious of the fact that the U.S.S.R. has never followed the rules, has always played very rough and for keeps, and that it is deadly serious as well as formidable.
To my mind the main causes of world unrest and instability today are twofold: First, the rise of nationalism and the justifiable desire for complete sovereignty in many new nations of the world today. This is, of course, part of the natural evolution of nations and peoples which cannot and should not be objected to. A great deal of strife could be avoided by helping rather than by hindering them in their achievement of their natural goal. Canada could play, of course, as the minister stated, a tremendous role in this field because, having achieved independence by peaceful means, never having been an imperial power, having no axes to grind with any other nations in the world, those countries do not fear Canada; indeed, they trust her to be objective and impartial as well as sympathetic.
The second and main cause of world unrest and tension is the evident deadlock between the world's two most powerful nations, each championing its own different political ideology. Neither, of course, is willing to give way and the rest of the nations of the world just watch and wonder what the outcome will be. It is about this second cause of world tension that I should like to say a few words.
It has been stated many times by this government and by the previous government that the United Nations is one of the cornerstones of Canadian foreign policy. However, because of the lack of authoritative power of the United Nations the western powers have had to resort to defence organizations such as NATO and NORAD. Canada's participation in both these organizations is certainly justified, and indeed vital, but the very existence of these auxiliary organizations points out the serious weaknesses to be found in the United Nations organization itself, and it is these weaknesses that I believe should be analysed thoroughly and
6322	HOUSE OF
Supply-External Affairs objectively and from a study of these weaknesses we might achieve, perhaps unusual but workable solutions for greater world stability.
I am convinced that no country will willingly seek out a nuclear war but I am not convinced that our present attitude toward international relationships and the present lack of confidence and trust among the nations of the world is the best road to peace. I feel very strongly that the indecisions, the lack of determination, the mistrust, the fears that plague the member nations of the United Nations and thwart the useful decisions of the United Nations in the political field come about because of the undisputed fact that the member nations of the United Nations, as indeed all nations of the world, have today no political life of their own but live and breathe in the shadow of two powerful nations, each representing two completely opposite political ideologies, each having its own circle of sympathetic nations and each having its national prestige to maintain. The intense rivalry between these two nations, whether we are willing to admit it or not, is alone responsible for the international political climate and tension that exists throughout the world today.
The two powerful nations, of course, are the United States and the U.S.S.R.; the two competing ideologies are capitalism and communism. The sympathetic nations are the western countries and the satellite countries. The national prestige that each of these two giants has to maintain can be translated in materialistic terms of strength of armament, of scientific accomplishments, of national production, of economic strength and power. The strategic deployment of this power at the least provocation by one or the other of these two world giants as a justification of their respective political ideologies has not only caused fear and instability among the older nations of the world, but it has caused indecision and confusion among the newer nations who have only recently attained their sovereignty and who cannot help but hesitate as to which of those two political ideologies they will embrace. Unconsciously, perhaps, these nations, as indeed all the nations of the world, are waiting for the outcome of a decisive clash between these two world powers.
It is this final physical clash between the U.S.A. and the U.S.S.R. which must be avoided at all costs because it cannot and will not solve any existing international problems, and can only create greater problems, greater fears and greater distrust among nations. I have never heard it said that young giants have ever excelled in diplomacy and negotiations; they have never been trained to


negotiate closely or to compromise because their strength and power were to them sufficient justification in attaining their objectives. Although this might have been efficient it was seldom just and always dangerous. Giants have always been the exceptions and the rest of mortals have had to temper their desires, and even their justifiable ambitions, to what could be obtained by compromise and diplomacy, and it was under those conditions that the maximum of stability could be maintained.
Unless we are willing to concede that might is right, then we must avoid a showdown of strength between the U.S. and the U.S.S.R. as proof of the soundness of their respective political systems and substitute some other criterion which might not only avoid a nuclear war but which would be a more reasonable, a more practicable and indeed a more civilized basis on which to compare the intrinsic values of both political ideologies. Surely, strength of arms cannot be accepted as a true criterion of political philosophy by rational people.
And then, too Mr. Chairman, are we so sure that the only political systems available to the countries of the world, particularly to the new countries, are to be found only at either extreme of a political philosophy that we would be willing to destroy the world in an attempt to prove which of the extremes is the better? Because of the tremendous differences in the economic and social structures of nations I do not believe that absolute standards can be applied successfully in every case, nor do I believe that the nations of the world have no other alternative but to choose between either communism or capitalism. If the nations were free to adopt political systems which best corresponded to the needs of the people and to the circumstances of their countries, the political systems would range from one extreme to another, and that to me is as it should be.
I think the world by its rather passive role as spectator in the growing conflicts between the United States and the U.S.S.R. has placed both these countries in a most unfair position in forcing the two most powerful nations in the world, who psychologically cannot help vying with each other in the military field as well as in the economic, scientific and political fields, to decide upon and to determine what political and economic system will prevail throughout the countries of the world. If you take away all the frills, you realize that that indeed has been the nub of the international problem that has plagued the world since 1945.
Each giant is striving today with increased ardour and aggressiveness to win as many nations to its cause as possible. Each is highly

sensitive to rebukes, each is jealously guarding its international prestige and afraid of losing face, each is striving to attain a strategic advantage over the other. Both are carried away by righteous indignation to the point of brinkmanship and the tempo is increasing with the result that because of specific activities about which we read every day the world is being carried closer and closer to open warfare.
If instead of pushing the United States and the U.S.S.R. into the limelight of a deadly political ring as we are now doing the nations of the world, whether satellite countries or western countries, assumed the responsibilities which are rightly theirs and acted as a group with energy and determination in their own best interests, they would become an effective and, indeed, a necessary counterbalance to the world's two greatest powers.
It is clear that the interest of all nations of the world, because of marked economic, social and, indeed, cultural differences, is not necessarily that of either the United States or the U.S.S.R. I cannot help but believe that the nations of the world other than the United States and the U.S.S.R. have many common problems and many common interests. I also believe that between satellite countries and the western powers, other than the United States and the U.S.S.R., there is much more in common than the differences that may arise because of their respective policital systems, and I feel certain that agreement and understanding could be reached among these nations far more easily than between the United States and the U.S.S.R. I cannot but believe also that both the United States and the U.S.S.R. would be secretly relieved to be taken off the horns of a dilemma that could result in a war which I am sure neither country wants and that they would not object but would indeed welcome the initiative of holding informal meetings and discussions of problems common to all the other nations of the world. In this way we would perhaps relieve them in part at least from an almost unbearable responsibility.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has spoken of the independent stand that Canada is to take in international affairs, and although we have as yet seen no evidence of this perhaps the minister might consider extending an invitation to all the countries of the world, excluding only the U.S.S.R. and the United States, to send a responsible representative to an informal consultative meeting of nations to be held in camera in the parliament buildings at Ottawa as soon as possible for the purpose of discussing what role these nations can play to avert the
Supply-External Affairs catastrophic war that is becoming more and more imminent, and to study the possibility and the best way of forming an effective and practicable counterbalance, within the United Nations preferably or outside it if necessary, to these two world powers between whom there now exists an extremely dangerous and explosive tension.
I do not in the least underestimate the difficulties involved in my suggestion and I have a pretty good idea of what criticism will be levelled at it. But I cannot help but feel that owing to the seriousness of the situation as it exists today the response of nations to the invitation and, indeed, the suggestions that will be made during the meeting could indeed be surprising and extremely useful. It would seem to me that since the powerful nations of the world have not been able to bring world peace and stability and the conferences at the summit have proven to be ineffectual because of rivalry in power, perhaps the united strength and indeed the wisdom of the majority of nations of the world, who have no axes to grind and are not handicapped by being in the limelight, might put them in a far better position to find a surer and more stable road to lasting world peace which I feel sure every nation, including the United States and the U.S.S.R., earnestly desires.

maintopic: CANADIAN REACTION TO SOVIET DISARMAMENT PROPOSALS OF JUNE 2, 1960
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with the greatest interest to the addresses made this afternoon. Not only were they interesting but they were all marked with a degree of high seriousness which seems to me appropriate to the occasion. As Tom Paine said of his day, these are times which try men's souls, and surely we can subscribe to that point of view. Certainly it is a time for cool heads and stout hearts, a time for avoiding that danger which sees a reverse as a catastrophe and a setback as a disaster.
Having faith enough to believe that we creatures of this earth have a future despite our own worst efforts at times, I should like to deal briefly with what might be described as a more long range aspect of Canadian foreign policy. I was greatly interested in what the Secretary of State for External Affairs said about the Latin American area. I welcomed his statement to the effect that a Latin American division is being set up in his department, that moves are being made on the diplomatic front in the Central American region and, most of all, that Canada proposes to send an observer to the forthcoming conference at Quito. I recall the minister dealing with the interest he found in Latin America and the questions that were raised there as to Canada's non-membership in the organization of American states.
6324	HOUSE OF
Supply-External Affairs
Some years ago another Canadian cabinet minister visited South America. He came back and said that he found all South America desirous that Canada should enter the PanAmerican union. That was Mr. McKinnon, minister of trade and commerce at that time, who made an extensive and helpful tour in that area some years ago. Canada, as has been pointed out today, is a member of a good many international organizations and has actively and splendidly discharged its duties to them. Yet we are not a member of the organization in our own hemisphere, the oldest peaceful international organization in the world.
The organization of American states as it is now called was set up formally in 1889-90. It existed in an informal way prior to that time, but it is doubtful whether we could have been a member because we did not have independence. But then even if we could have been a member there is not much likelihood that we would have been welcome. The secretary of state of the United States wrote to the president at the time:
The fact is we do not want any intercourse with Canada except through the medium of the tariff and she will find she has a hard row to hoe and will ultimately, I believe, seek admission to the union.
This was secretary of state Blaine who was once described by his political opponents as "Blaine, Blaine, the continental liar from the State of Maine". I would not comment on his veracity at all even though he is now an historic figure. But, I must say, he was not very profound as a prophet. But 20 years later great changes had come in the United States and Blaine's successor Eliuh Root, who presided over the building of the PanAmerican union building, suggested that in the inner cornice of that building the coat of arms of Canada be placed and that a Canadian panel be set up in the board room. Indeed it is said that a chair was ordered in which the Canadian representative would some day sit. I have seen the coat of arms. It is not a very good one in that it shows the arms of only the four original provinces, which does not include Prince Edward Island. The chair I have not seen but it is said that the optimism of Mr. Root's was expressed in this practical way.
In 1909 the director of the Pan-American union was in Ottawa and he discussed Canada's membership with Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier. The prime minister was enthusiastic about Canada's future membership but he thought it would be impractical at that time. During the years this machinery was improved, developed, headquarters were set up at Washington, a bureaucracy established. But for a long time it was not a very viable poli-
[Mr. Macquarrle.l

tlcal international organization, continually under the domination of the United States, a veto placed on political discussion because in all candor we must admit there were certain activities of the United States in the hemispheric field at that time which her ministers would probably not relish being discussed in international gatherings. This was the era of the taking of the canal, the era of the expansion of marine activity in the central and West Indies areas, the era of the dollar diplomacy, the Monroe doctrine and other aspects of United States policy in respect to Latin America.
If United States popularity in Latin America reached its nadir under Teddy Roosevelt it was under another Roosevelt that it reached its zenith. The good neighbour policy of Franklin D. Roosevelt inaugurated an era of understanding and of co-operation. This international machinery became truly a hemispheric body. No longer did it function as an adjunct to the state department. The Latin American states took their place in the most prominent committees and boards. The Latin American outlook was given expression. Political discussions were encouraged and the United States, with great wisdom, abandoned many of the policies which had made it unpopular in the hemisphere and which had prevented it from becoming a true leader in this hemisphere despite its great material, physical and military strength. The colossus of the north by its own wisdom decided to pursue policies which enhanced its prestige and strengthened its position. Today this organization now called the organization of American states exists as a regional agency under section 52 of the U.N. charter with a highly developed group of specialized organizations and agencies to many of which Canada belongs. Indeed, this country participated in specialized agencies as early as 1893. All the ad hoc arrangements were brought up to date in 1948 in the Bogota charter, as it is called, the charter of the O.A.S., which now functions as the basic document of this hemispheric organization to which 21 states belong. An agreement of mutual assistance was entered into in 1947 providing for mutual defence of the hemisphere and interestingly enough including in that area the territory of Canada. At one time the United States attitude was hostility toward our admission. At a later date it was indifference. Then came a desire to have us join and I think that change found its most eloquent expression in the splendid invitation issued by Senator Vandenburg:
By every rule of righteousness she Is eligible to this association. By every rule of reason we should wish her here. I should welcome the final and total New World unity which will be nobly

dramatized when the twenty second chair is filled and our continental brotherhood is complete from the Arctic circle to Cape Horn.
Decision as to the question of our eligibility has long since been made. We are, of course, a sovereign nation with many international commitments. I think there is no reason to doubt that our welcome would be genuine, sincere and universal. The question now is this. Should Canada take that chair? In my brash youth I once suggested that membership in the Pan-American union, as it was called, would be a good thing. In discussing external affairs last session I gave voice to the same opinion. As I grow older I am more convinced that this is a good move and an important one.
In Canada, as the minister said earlier, there has long been a lack of interest in the hemisphere beyond the Rio Grande. Over the years in this chamber there have been a few members who have spoken about Canada's membership in the hemispheric organization. J. S. Woodsworth and Miss Agnes MacPhail were strong advocates of our membership. I ran across an interesting speech by the hon. member for Essex East which I should like to use to adorn this dull discourse but because of the hour I will desist. Mr. Coldwell was another one who approved. Members of the Conservative party at times also spoke on this matter.
I think it is a happy thing to encourage interest in this field and I am very pleased that King's University in Halifax is developing a Latin American institute. I think that is a forward step and it is one which I heartily welcome. Some who talk about membership in the Pan-American union would say that we are not intimately concerned about this part of the world. They would say it is the northern hemisphere or it is the commonwealth tie that should concern us. One cannot in this modern world rope off an area and say "In this part we are not interested". As the minister so rightly said, anyone is 24 hours away from anyone else in this modern world. Gone is the day when any Canadian can say, as one once did say: We live in a fireproof house far from inflammable material, why should we pay high insurance premiums?
Peace, stability and prosperity of the whole western hemisphere are a matter of real interest and concern to us. To those who say "Don't get involved" I can only say in all candor, "We are involved". Where are the frontiers of any state today? I remember Prime Minister Baldwin making a statement that Britain's frontiers were now on the Rhine. Where are ours? Are there any of these distant and remote countries, as
Supply-External Affairs Mr. Chamberlain once inanely described Czechoslovakia just before the second war broke at that time? The people of Latin America are our friends, people with whom we work closely at the United Nations and elsewhere. Twenty members of that body are Latin American. Their influence I believe is even greater than that figure would indicate. It is an area which produces a great sense of real international feeling.
One might talk about sociological similarities. We, like they, are new world states where we have transplanted our old world traditions; and again we, like they, are dedicated to the free world because in these present tense days, although within our inner structures we differ one from the other, I think one can say that the free world today needs all its friends in as friendly a mood as possible.
Perhaps I might deal with the question of trade. In 1938 our exports to the Latin American world were something over $19 million. In 1948 they had risen to $132 million, and in 1958 to $180 million. Our imports have risen from $23 million to $350 million. That is not as high as they might be, and indeed steps might be taken both by the Latin Americans and ourselves to foster an expansion of trade. I think that increased trade might better further both the social and political contacts between us.
Another reaction that one has seen to a suggestion of Canada's participation in this hemispheric organization might be described as a holier than thou attitude. Sometimes one reads of the tendency of these countries toward dictators and of the primitive nature of their political institutions. And of course we have to recognize immediately that it would be folly to judge their political and social societies by our own values and standards. But even by those I think we could say that political democracy in general in Latin America is stronger today than ever before.
But then, to be realistic, if we take this holier than thou attitude toward other countries, what international organization could we belong to if disapproval of their form of government should cause us to abstain? In recent days I have seen reports in the papers which are interested and do not shy away from the question about the events in the republic of Cuba. It would be highly unfortunate if we should miss all the accomplishments of Pan-Americanism in our concentration on the excesses and exercises of the present ruler of that particular nation. Looking back over its history we could see that this hemisphere has survived somewhat similar threats before. Indeed, I am inclined to

Supply-External Affairs believe that the events in Cuba should cause us to look all the more closely at these hemispheric developments.
It is not for me to discuss the internal politics of Cuba or any other country; nor has the Canadian government, or as far as I know the Canadian people, interfered in any way with the changes that appeared to be taking place some months ago in this country. Yet it should be recalled that Pan-Americanism had its origin in an effort to bring co-operation and unity and greater strength within the hemisphere against a threat from without. The spiritual father of the Pan-American movement was the great liberator Simon Bolivar. In 1826 he saw that these new American states were in danger from activity across the waters and he thought that by bringing them together, from their unity would come the strength of survival. There are far greater threats from across the waters today than ever existed in the nineteenth century in Bolivar's time.
The evil effects of communist encroachment in Cuba would be visited not only upon the people of Cuba but upon the whole hemisphere, and one of the first casualties would be this whole system of hemispheric solidarity and co-operation which has been built up so successfully and largely on the basis of Latin American leadership and inspiration. One can but hope that that same leadership will be aware of the grave dangers which would come to any transgressions by a hostile and alien force.
Then again one hears the regrettable argument that it would be unfortunate if Canada should join the organization of American states, because once in that organization we might find ourselves in disagreement with the United States or lining up against Latin America. This argument is almost contemptible. To suggest that such a thing would deter us is unworthy. We have disagreed with the United States before and have so far survived. The reluctance to enter any organization because we might fear that at some time a situation would arise where there would not be unanimity is to me a most wishy-washy notion and is not really deserving serious consideration.
It has been said at times that our membership in the commonwealth should preclude our membership in the organization of the United States. This, I think, is a holdover from thinking which was prevalent in the days before we attained full national sovereignty. I would look forward to the day when not one member of the commonwealth but two would take their place in the organization of American states and act as an important liaison between two very important
[Mr. Macquarrie.I
and very valuable international bodies in the world today. The second member I think of would be the Federation of the West Indies.
But there is another side to this. Not only should we ask ourselves, what can we get out of it; what will it mean in terms of economics and increased trade, in terms of increased prestige in the councils of the world? A country like Canada with its values and ideals might ask, what can we contribute rather than what can we get? -One hon. member mentioned earlier in the debate the important contributions which Canada was able to make in the international field. He outlined many reasons for this, one being the lack of a legacy of ill will which some other countries may have.
It seems to me we are uniquely qualified to perform usefully and helpfully in this hemispheric organization. We are not without experience in dealing with a powerful and in earlier times somewhat expansionist neighbour. We can recall some instances which are similar to those which occurred between Latin America and the United States. We, like they, have passed into a period where complete independence has meant an improvement in relations and the strengthening of the bonds of friendship, a situation indeed which prevailed throughout the various stages of our development with our former mother country and our great ally and friend, the United Kingdom.
We are a country, like many countries in Latin America, with great national resources yet to be developed. We have that common situation. We are a country with an advanced technology and a mature economy, a country which could move forward to greater things in association with these great peoples further to the south.
One might devote a good deal of time to discussing just this one aspect of our international relations. I think it would be worth while to do something more than simply hop from one crisis to another; we might undertake to do something the benefits of which would unfold as the years go by and allow us to make a greater contribution to the world beyond our own shores.
I think Canadian membership in this organization would be warmly welcomed by both Latin America and the United States. I think our joining it would be a move which would benefit both ourselves and our neighbours. It would strengthen the peaceful purposes of a very important part of the world and it would be a contribution to stability and to international goodwill. I do not think we should now miss the opportunity which is presented to us, and if the government should

decide to play its full part in this organization I think the people of Canada would welcome the move. I look forward to the day when we shall occupy this twenty second chair and accept the full responsibilities of our position as a free state in the western hemisphere. I hope Canada will be at the conference as an observer, and that this will open the door to full-fledged participation in this important international body.

maintopic: CANADIAN REACTION TO SOVIET DISARMAMENT PROPOSALS OF JUNE 2, 1960
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
In taking part in this debate on external affairs I do so for the purpose of making a few comments regarding the question of territorial and fishing limits and to comment also on the conference which was held at Geneva a few months ago.
I believe we have reached the time in Canada when to protect our fishing interests some system of uniform maritime regulations is required. Such international regulations of territorial and fishing limits are of the utmost importance to Canada. Along the coasts of Canada lie many old and historic fishing grounds which for generations, indeed for centuries, have provided rich harvest for our people as well as for those of many other countries. On the west coast of Canada we have the United States fishing for salmon and halibut with our own fishermen. On the east coast of Canada we have France, Spain, Portugal, Russia and many other countries fishing with the fishermen of eastern Canada. Hon. members will remember that a few years ago in 1956 there was a celebration at St. John's, Newfoundland which marked the five hundredth annual expedition of the Portuguese to the Grand Banks off Newfoundland.
Canada is one of the largest fish producing nations in the world. In these years the annual catch by Canadians is in the vicinity of two billion pounds having a gross value of about $100 million. The value of these fisheries is emphasized when we compare the total catch with those of other countries with far greater populations. For example, the United Kingdom, with three times our population, has about the same annual catch. The United States, with ten times our population, has only three times our annual production of fish" products. But while it may be important to compare the total annual production of our fisheries with the annual production of other nations and also with the total production of all commodities in our own country, it may be of still greater value in a country of such wide expanse as Canada to compare the regional value of the fisheries with the total production of the area in which they are operated.
There are indications that in the years which lie ahead markets for fishery products 79951-0-399
Supply-External Affairs will become highly competitive. In recent years many countries in order to increase employment and to provide greater sources of protein and secure a greater share of world markets have made real efforts to expand their fishing industry, As a result, over the five-year period from 1953 to 1958 world production increased from 25 million metric tons to 34 million metric tons, or an increase of 35 per cent. In the same period Canadian production has remained relatively stable.
Here two points are of interest to Canada. First, that the fishing industry in Canada is not maintaining its position among the countries of the world and, second, that some of the nations which have contributed to the increase in world production have secured a large percentage of their increased production from waters off the Pacific and Atlantic coasts of Canada.
Canada's share in the total catch in the northwest Atlantic is gradually decreasing while foreign vessels become more numerous each year. More than 160 Russian ships up to 14,000 tons each, and with crews totalling 25,000, are, during the present season, off the banks of Newfoundland. This figure is 30 per cent higher than the total number of fishermen in the province of Newfoundland. Also in the area are 60 Portuguese vessels, with 6,000 fishermen, together with 80 ships from Spain with more than 2,500 crew members. Obviously these operations will have an effect on world markets, and may tend to dislodge our exports which account for two-thirds of our total catch.
I hasten to say that I am not arguing that these ships when on the Grand Banks are within the proposed 12-mile limit. The point I am making is that if other nations are attributing such importance to the prosecution of the fisheries that is all the more reason why the fishery resources within the 12-mile limit on both coasts of Canada should be protected.
These regulations are important to Canada for other reasons. We live in a country with an increasing population. Since 1956 our population has increased by 1.5 million, or 9.9 per cent. About one third of our population is 15 years of age or under, and 40 per cent of our population is less than 20 years of age. We must anticipate here in Canada a much larger population and at the same time look forward to some means whereby employment can be provided for these people.
These regulations regarding territorial and fishing limits are important for another reason. Canada may be the only country in the world which has its borders on three great oceans, the Atlantic on the east, the

Supply-External Affairs Pacific on the west and the Arctic on the north. It has a coastline of 60,000 miles, one of the two longest in the world. Canada is one of the largest trading nations in the world exporting annually to all parts of the globe about 50 million tons of cargo. A nation such as ours must consider regulations governing territorial and fishing rights to be of extreme importance.
The Hague conference of 1930 was in many ways similar to the two conferences of more recent years. It called for codifications of the law of the sea. Forty nations attended that conference but the conference broke down on the question of territorial limits. Since then, and in the absence of international law on this question, many nations have unilaterally declared limits to their own territorial sea. The three-mile limit has less validity now than it had in 1930. Many other aspects of the law of the sea demonstrate the need for a codification of these laws.
In 1947 the United Nations formed the international law commission. Ten years later that commission, after a very exhaustive study of virtually every aspect of the law of the sea, presented its report covering the whole topic of maritime law. As a result of this report the United Nations in February 1957 called for a conference to be held in Geneva in 1958. We will remember that that conference was held from February 24 to April 28. Eighty-six nations were present. This conference produced four conventions covering some 74 articles. By no stretch of the imagination could this conference be considered as a failure. Many of those things which were done at this conference needed to be done and gave to the countries of the world some definite direction in maritime matters.
No such conference is a failure because it does not reach agreement on all the points on its agenda but it is a success only in so far as it makes progress in the desired direction. True it is that the first conference was not a complete success but if it was not a complete success it was a notable success. It was not a complete success because it failed to reach agreement on territorial and fishing limits.
The position taken by Canada at that time was similar to the position stated by the Canadian delegation at the United Nations in 1956. At the second conference the position of Canada outlined in the booklet tabled by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and distributed earlier this year was made very clear. May I at this point commend the minister for this very fine booklet.

I think this booklet gave to people in other countries a very clear conception of what the Canadian stand was but I also believe it gave to our own people an excellent conception of where Canada stood in this very important matter.
I believe that the question of territorial limits should be a separate and distinct question from that of fishing limits. The absence of international law has led many states to take unilateral action in extending their own territorial and fishing limits to protect what they consider to be their own national interests. All states have a responsibility to safeguard the interests of their own people but when such action interferes with the freedom of others then a re-examination of the pertinent sections of international law becomes urgent.
For many years Canada like many other countries has adhered to the three-mile limit. Other states, on the other hand, have expressed the idea that the three-mile limit is no longer adequate to serve what might be considered their reasonable interests. Obviously the problem is to find some common ground for conciliation between the special interests of states on the one hand and the concept of the freedom of the seas on the other.
The international law commission expressed the opinion at the first conference that there was no legal permission for states to extend their territorial limits beyond 12 miles. Because of this there are those who contend that nations have the right to determine their own territorial limits up to 12 miles. Such contentions are not conducive to uniform practice and tend to develop uncertainty in international affairs. Other nations have supported the idea of a 12-mile territorial limit. While such a suggestion of implemented would offer a solution to some problems it might in some areas reduce the freedom of trade and commerce which we now enjoy.
For example, if a 12-mile territorial limit were accepted by the conference 116 important international straits would become territorial waters of some country and of these 18 would come under the authority of countries which might indeed terminate or interfere with the free passage of ships of some other countries. Even if the territorial limit were only extended to six miles there would still be 52 such international straits which would come under national jurisdiction but only 11 of these might have any tendency toward curtailing the free passage of ships.
Many nations are fortunate in having great fishery resources in the waters surrounding

their coasts. It is understandable that these nations would want to conserve these resources against depletion in order to maintain any existing fishing industry they may have as a source of employment and exports. When fishery jurisdiction is being considered not only the question of conservation must be kept in mind but also that of the utilization of the coastal fisheries. It may be that in one area all the conservation measures may be observed in order to maintain a sustainable yield and yet that total yield may not be of sufficient quantity to meet all the demands which may be made upon it. Surely in such a case a country should in some way attempt to protect its own interests.
For example, Iceland's economy demands that nearly all the necessities of life have to be imported. These imports have to be financed through exports which are 97 per cent fisheries products. Fishing limits in some countries have seen considerable changes over the years. In the 17th century in Iceland these limits were 32 miles. Later they were reduced to 24 miles and in the 19th century to 16 miles. At the close of the last century foreign pressure was sufficient to force the recognition of a 14-mile limit. In 1901 by agreement with the United Kingdom, a 10-mile rule in bays and a three-mile limit around the island became recognized. This agreement was terminated by Iceland in 1951, and I know that hon. members are well acquainted with the results of the termination of that agreement.
It is necessary to find some compromise between the views of nations with commercial fishing fleets operating far from their own shores and those nations with large fishery resources in the waters around their own shores. In their own interests and in the absence of international law many nations have declared fishing limits. For example, in 1906 Norway declared her limit to be four miles; in 1907 Argentina, 12 miles; in 1909 Spain, six miles; in 1912 Italy, seven miles; in 1914 Greece, six miles; in 1923 Colombia, 12 miles; in 1933 Ecuador, 15 miles; in 1938 Brazil, 12 miles; in 1949 Costa Rica, 200 miles; in 1951 Korea 50 to 60 miles; in 1952 the Dominican Republic, 12 miles; in 1955 El Salvador, 200 miles; in 1957 Cambodia, 12 miles; India 100 miles; Ceylon 100 miles. I have given these figures to point out that although many of us may believe that the three-mile limit is one that is observed by most nations, the fact is that these figures prove that many nations have not observed the three-mile limit but have gone well beyond it.
In the fall of 1958, at the United Nations when the nations discussed the possibility 79951-0-399J
Supply-External Affairs of having a second conference on the law of the sea, of the 80-odd nations then present only about 20 of them were observing a three-mile limit.
In 1911, Canada declared that as a conservation measure trawlers over 65 feet in length should not be permitted to operate inside the 12-mile limit. This regulation was applied to Canadian boats and for almost half a century we have denied to our own fishermen a right which has been accorded to the fishermen of every other nation on earth.
When fishing limits in areas of other nations engaged in the industry are discussed there arises the question of historic fishing rights which are honoured either by custom or by treaty. In the northwestern Atlantic there have been a number of treaties dealing with these rights which played such an important and significant role in the discussions at both Geneva conferences. For example, in 1783 there was a treaty recognizing the independence of the United States of America, but it also provided among other things that United States subjects should have the same rights as those granted to British seamen on all coasts.
In 1818 there was agreement that the citizens of the United States should have forever the right to catch fish of all kinds in waters around the then colony of Newfoundland and in waters along the east and northeast coasts of Canada, with the exception of certain rights of the Hudson's Bay Company.
In 1823 there were discussions between the British and the United States governments dealing wih difficulties in the areas of the bay of Chaleur and the bay of Fundy. In 1854 the reciprocity treaty settled some of those difficulties and produced an agreement for the duration of 10 years and termination by notice of one of the contracting parties.
In 1866 the required notice was given to the government of the United States and the reciprocity treaty was terminated on March 17.
During the years in the 18th and 19th centuries fishing rights in Newfoundland, then a British colony, were subject to changes and modifications by a number of treaties. I do not propose to make any further comment on those treaties at this time, Mr. Chairman, but they do add to the long history of fishing rights on Canada's Atlantic coast.
On July 20, 1912, an agreement of major importance was signed between the British government and the government of the United States of America dealing with north Atlantic fisheries as well as confirming some aspects of the special agreements signed between the two countries on April 4, 1908.

Supply-External Affairs
Canada's position in the last conference recognized the importance of historic fishing rights by suggesting a period of 10 years during which time historic rights within the proposed 12-mile limit could be terminated. This, in my opinion, was a fair compromise. My own province of Newfoundland has always had a particular interest in fishing limits. Perhaps no other part of Canada, on either coast, has been subjected to the long history of fishing treaties and regulations as has the province of Newfoundland. From the early days of the fishing admirals to the present day, our fishermen have been aware of the importance of limits to protect the inshore fishery and to reserve it for those whose livelihood depended upon this particular type of fishing. Today the inshore fishery is not protected from large draggers, except within the three-mile limit, either from foreign countries or from other Canadian areas. Many of our fishermen allege that grounds, even within the three-mile limit, are sometimes destroyed or to a measure depleted by vessels equipped to fish in deeper waters. Fears of what may happen were expressed in the convention of the federation of fishermen of Newfoundland last November. This attitude was well stated in an editorial in the St. John's Telegram of November 9, 1959, which I should like to quote, Mr. Chairman:
The delegates to the federation of fishermen convention are alarmed and rightly so about the "tremendous tonnage" of fish being taken off the northeast coast by foreign fishing fleets. They fear such inroads may destroy the large bodies of breeding codfish known to be concentrated in that area from which most of Newfoundland's inshore fishery is supplied. The result could be the loss of that fishery which is the economic mainstay of thousands of Newfoundland families.
Ships from every maritime country in the world, not satisfied with the Vast resources of the banks of Newfoundland, penetrate our territorial waters, well inside the three-mile limit to fish.
Most people are aware that the visits of these foreign trawlers bring a certain amount of business to this province, apart altogether from the purchase of bait supplies. But events are moving to a point where the whole question may have to be examined to see if the advantages on the one hand outweigh the disadvantages on the other. While the fishery of Newfoundland does not constitute anything like 97 per cent of the economy as in Iceland, nevertheless it is a vital factor in the over-all economic set-up.
Indications are that it is taking a new lease on life and serious account must be taken of international or local developments that may hinder its progress.
The second conference on the law of the sea which opened in Geneva in March of this year held out considerable hope that progress would be made on the two fundamental questions of territorial and fishing limits. Many who followed the proceedings of the first conference and noted the discussions at

the meeting of the United Nations in 1958 considered that there was a real possibility of arriving at some satisfactory solution to this most vexing question. The position taken by the different countries was well stated beforehand with the result that when the conference opened it did so with a clear understanding of the problems before it.
I believe that the Canadian six plus six formula was the only alternative to the proposal of a 12-mile territorial sea and, if agreement had been reached, not only would there have been a great stride forward by the international community in maritime matters but the codification of the law of the sea would have been completed. The Canadian proposal, even after being amended to provide a period of 10 years during which time historic fishing rights would remain in force, failed to get the necessary two-thirds support from the 87 nations represented at Geneva. Fifty four nations voted in favour, 28 nations against and five abstained. One more vote in favour would have carried the proposal which would then have been international law. By one vote the nations disagreed on territorial and fishing rights for the third time in 30 years.
Of the 15 NATO nations who were present all voted for the proposal except Iceland. Of the commonwealth countries who were present all voted in favour of the Canadian proposal except India. The opposition came mainly from the soviet bloc together with the African, Asian and Latin American groups who favoured universal extension of territorial waters to 12 miles.
Following the decision many of the big maritime nations indicated their intention to withdraw their support for the Canadian proposal and stated that they would not recognize the unilateral claim of any nation to a jurisdiction beyond the traditional three miles. Mr. Arthur Dean, the United States delegate, commenting on the result of the second conference, said: "It seems we go back to the old chaos". The United Kingdom delegate, Mr. John Hare, said that the failure of the conference "will face the world with many great problems which could have been solved".
What is Canada's position now? In the light of the results of the second conference, what is the position of the other maritime nations of the world? Some nations have indicated their intention of recognizing nothing but the traditional three-mile limit and argue that under present international law they are forced to recognize for other nations nothing more than the limits which they proclaim for themselves. For example, if a nation declares

its own limits to be three miles then it is not required to observe any more than three miles around the shores of any other nation. Others will contend that there is no breach of international law in extending their limits to any distance up to 12 miles. Obviously the stage is set for a good deal of misunderstanding and increased international tensions.
On May 13, 1960, following the results of the Geneva conference, the foreign minister of Norway announced in a speech in parliament that Norway would extend her fishing limits from four to 12 miles. This action will certainly not go unnoticed in Ottawa and I suspect it will not go unnoticed in the capitals of other maritime countries which have fishing industries to protect.
What action will the government now take? Will it be possible and, if so, how effective will it be to arrive at some agreement between those 54 nations who voted for the Canadian proposal at the second Geneva conference? Or there may be some merit in attempting to arrive at agreements with those countries fishing in Canadian waters, including Russia, the United States, the United Kingdom, Portugal, Spain and Norway. In such a case Canada might have to permit these nations to fish up to some prescribed limit for a few years and then gradually increase the limit to 12 miles while efforts are being made to find fishing grounds outside that area.
There may be some advantage into entering into negotiations with those nations participating in regional fishery conventions. Even though limited this would still be an improvement over the present situation. A north Atlantic fishery convention, where fishing limits could be discussed by those concerned, would have some attraction. This might take some considerable time but might provide answers, in some measure at least, to many of the problems which now beset maritime countries.
For example, in the Icelandic dispute Britain has now offered to begin further discussions with a view to terminating gradually her historic rights to fish in waters off Iceland. Certainly some such plan might be effective for the waters off the east coast of Canada. Canada might adopt a similar course and in the absence of any international law enter into negotiations with those countries who voted for the Canadian proposal at Geneva or with those who, either by custom or agreement, have traditionally fished off the Canadian coast.
Finally, Canada could by unilateral action declare her fishing limits to be 12 miles. It may be that in the blush of disappointment after the second Geneva conference there
Supply-External Affairs would be many people who would say that this is what we must do, that we must extend our fishing limits unilaterally to 12 miles. But maybe on sober reflection, when we take into account the position of Canada within the international community and also take into account our position as an exporter of two thirds of our total fishery production, we should take another look at such a proposition and decide that such action should only be taken as a last resort.
Most people will agree that the sea should be open to all but at the same time will recognize the need for coastal states to exercise sovereignty over a narrow belt along their coasts. The present three-mile limit is neither practicable nor realistic. In addition, it seems to me there should be special consideration in areas where observance of conservation measures is urgently required or where the economy of isolated populations is to an exceptionally high degree dependent on the resources of the sea.
Whatever policy the government proposes to adopt, two facts must be borne in mind. First, Canada has fishery resources which must be protected. The present 12-mile regulation relating to Canadian trawlers in some areas provides very little protection when foreign vessels have rights which are denied to our own fishermen. Second, such protection as is required cannot be provided by accepting the failure of the second Geneva conference as the final answer but by continually pressing for a solution to this most disturbing problem and adopting as firm an attitude as the circumstances of the case require.

maintopic: CANADIAN REACTION TO SOVIET DISARMAMENT PROPOSALS OF JUNE 2, 1960
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I think the hon. member for Humber-St. George's is to be congratulated upon the presentation he has just made on an important topic and one that has continued to exercise the attention of this chamber over the years. The subject with which I propose to deal tonight is in a slightly different vein and perhaps the hon. member will pardon me if I do not comment on his speech at this time.
The problem we face is this:
What sort of future are we trying to create for ourselves and our children? Is it to be better, or worse than that which we have inherited? Are we trying to make a world in which the peoples that inhabit it shall be able to live out their lives in peace of mind and in the enjoyment of a constantly rising standard of all that makes life worth living, of health and comfort, of recreation, and of culture? Or are we preparing for ourselves a future which is to be one perpetual nightmare, filled with the constant dread of the horrors of war, forced to bury ourselves below ground and to spend all our substance upon the weapons of destruction?
These words were not spoken today or even yesterday but they were uttered almost 23 years ago. They were words spoken in

Supply-External Affairs the first public speech made by Neville Chamberlain after he attained the office of prime minister of Great Britain. Summing up as they do the dreadul alternatives of his as well as our time, they place beside the "great and human yearning for peace" mentioned earlier today by the Secretary of State for External Affairs the nuclear madness that permeates the very air we breathe. Our problem is to assure the one without subjecting ourselves to the other.
It must never be forgotten that peace in freedom is our objective, the peace of free men, peace in freedom and not the peace of slaves. It is to this end that we must pursue courses that assure the end that Neville Chamberlain sought but that he did not reach because he and his country at that time were not willing to believe that peace without safeguards is an illusion and is just as unattainable as the mirage of the desert.
I say this because there is a danger that, in our anxiety to reach the goal we may forget the paths by which that goal may be reached, the pathways which we must build painstakingly across the morass of suspicion and hatred. We must protect our pathway as we build it against the undermining, the encroachment upon its foundations, of sly and subtle or ignorant or uninformed exhortations to weakness.
There is no short and easy road to peace. There is no short and easy way in which we can bridge the hostilities and the hatreds which have been built up by almost three generations of communist leaders. Nor is there any short and easy way in which we can allay our own suspicions, our own fears, founded as they are on many instances throughout many years of examples of the communist character, and on their declared aims and objectives to wrest from us by force, if necessary, control of the sacred institutions of freedom and liberty which are our heritage.
As the Secretary of State for External Affairs has said, in effect this is a task we must approach with optimism, sure in the knowledge that in all men's hearts the desires expressed by Neville Chamberlain find an echo. We shall not reach our goal by pessimism or by gloomy doubts, or by hope-denying postulations of pseudo-realism, for without perennial hope and without perpetual optimism we shall not have the heart, the will or the wit to complete our task. I say these things for from some quarters there have been suggestions that we should abandon our alliances, that we should forsake our friends in favour of a doubtful and defenceless position of neutrality.

These suggestions are of course not new, and although they have persistently arisen in the deliberations and suggestions of the C.C.F. party, they are not by any means restricted to that party alone. As hon. members may recall, the latest major effort in this field is "Peacemaker or Powder-Monkey" by James F. Minifie, an ex-patriate Canadian who incidentally warns us against the dangers of national expatriation. An echo of this view was reflected in a resolution passed by the C.C.F. convention of the Saskatoon constituency as reported in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix a couple of weeks ago. They called for the withdrawal of Canada from NATO. It was a resolution similar to one put forward by them last year and which, I am happy to say, was opposed by both Mr. Coldwell and Premier T. C. Douglas.
Freedom must be guarded if peace in freedom is to be assured. I go back to the days of 1937 when this proposition was ever on the lips of one to whom at that time the world paid no heed. Writing in his "History of the Second World War", in the volume entitled "The Gathering Storm", Sir Winston Churchill recalled:
We shall see how the councils of prudence and restraint may become the prime agents of mortal danger; how the quiet middle course adopted from desires for safety and a quiet life may be found to lead direct to the bull's eye of disaster. We shall see how absolute is the need of a broad path of international action pursued by many states in common across the years, irrespective of the ebb and flow of national politics.
To those who advocate the course of neutrality, the course of unilateral disarmament, the course of withdrawal from NATO, to those who continually heap strictures upon the United States, the United Kingdom and others with us in the vanguard of freedom, may I put these questions: Are we to disarm our friends? Are we to have no allies? Are we to neglect our own defences entirely and, at the same time, by struggling in this direction are we to weaken the unity of the forces that keep us free? This course would, indeed, lead us to a miserable and perilous situation. Indeed, Mr. Chairman, it was to guard against this outcome that NATO was formed. It was to guard against this result that NORAD was formed. To those who would have us dismantle the implements of our protection, may we point out the painful example of history.
On the subject of disarmament, may I recall the words of Sir Winston Churchill of July 13, 1934 as reported on page 102 of "The Gathering Storm". This was on the occasion of the indefinite adjournment of the

standing committee of the disarmament conference at Geneva, which happened in the course of June, 1934. He said this:
I am very glad that the disarmament conference is passing out of life into history. It is the greatest mistake to mix up disarmament with peace. When you have peace you will have disarmament. But there has been during these recent years a steady deterioration in the relations between different countries, a steady growth of ill-will, and a steady, indeed a rapid, increase in armaments that has gone on through all these years in spite of the endless flow of oratory, of perorations, of wellmeaning sentiments, of banquets, which have marked this epoch.
Europe will be secure when nations no longer feel themselves in great danger, as many of them do now. Then the pressure and the burden of armaments will fall away automatically, as they ought to have done in a long peace; and it might be quite easy to seal a movement of that character by some general agreement.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has set the first objective as the release from tension, and I think that is sound. It is broader in scope and it was indeed the context in which the latest disarmament committee worked, at least on our side. It must not be assumed that we can relieve tension by making ourselves weak, by disarming ourselves, by withdrawing from those alliances and agreements that add our efforts to a mutual arrangement for our security. Tension will not be relieved if their side remains strong and our side becomes weak. We have already had sufficient evidence since the war of what happens when the communist finds before him, like a pork chop on a plate, as it were, a weak and defenceless nation. The way to relieve tension is to remain strong; to make it abundantly clear that that strength stands ready for the defence of freedom, and at the same time to make absolutely certain to everyone in the world that that strength will never be used except for the defence of freedom.
When we get these two points across, when they become accepted, tension may be relieved in the security of peace. Then the activities of such disarmament committees as the most recent one may show their value in exploring the depths of the sincerity of the other side and of making manifest our own abiding determination to continue on the path to peace. But we would be quite wrong if we were to assume that disarmament committees and disarmament conferences were the only way in which the sincerities and the peaceful determinations of the two sides might be explored, tested and encouraged.
On the subject of aid to the less developed nations I recall again to hon. members of this committee the resolution agreed on by that great assembly of the Atlantic congress in London a year ago last June, which reads:
Our nations should form a partnership in freedom with the peoples of Africa, Asia and Latin America
Supply-External Affairs
for the great task of development of those continents. Our nations should provide a massive and sustained effort toward this end, believing it to be as essential to the well-being of the world as the welfare or the defence of our own citizens.
Much has been said by this government in that regard. Our aid has been increased, particularly under the Colombo plan, but in other ways as well. However, we must not forget that much more remains to be done, and it is significant to note that in that portion of the resolution which I have just quoted the emphasis was not that our governments alone should do these things, but that our nations should provide that massive and sustained effort that will bring a rising standard of living with the hope of individual freedom, human dignity and democratic institutions.
The efforts of this nation in this regard should not be left to the government alone, and in saying this I do not forget the valuable work which has been done by many associations, groups and private individuals in this general field. I am thinking particularly of our business and financial institutions, of our commercial organizations, and I am using that word in the broadest sense. Exports are rising. As at the end of May of this year they were over $250 million greater than for the same period last year; but the proportion of our manufactured and processed exports, the exports that provide more jobs for Canadians, has not risen in like proportion.
I am not getting on to the subject of trade, but in order to advance the proposition I wish to make it is necessary to refer to this fact in regard to our exports and I quote from an editorial in the Gazette of June 1 of this year:
The hard fact is that the average costs of manufacturing in Canada (excluding such primary industries as pulp and newsprint, where scale is no problem) run some 35 per cent to 40 per cent higher than in the United States.
This editorial goes on to say:
This difference in the cost of manufacturing is explained by the fact that the U.S. market is some 15 to 20 times as large as the Canadian market. U.S. manufacturers can obtain much greater economies of scale, with bigger production runs, more specialization in machinery and labour, and lower costs of overhead and distribution.
I might recall to the hon. members of this committee that this is so despite the disparity in wages paid in the two countries. To me this points to one solution. Our markets abroad for our manufactured and processed products must be expanded in order that the greater economies of scale which bigger production runs bring about may inure to the benefit of Canadians, not only the Canadians

Supply-External Affairs in those industries but all Canadians who will receive the advantage of the reduction in costs.
To this end I have suggested on several occasions that the time has come for the Canadian financial and business world to join actively in the general program for development of the less developed areas. Over a year ago, speaking to a group of Toronto businessmen, I suggested that they look to the underdeveloped areas for expansion and for profit. The initiative should be with them.
I do not underestimate the problems. The problems of governmental instability in underdeveloped areas is real, but so are the potential profits. In areas where the risk is greater because of instability and the possibility of nationalization, you may feel that the risk is greater than your capacity to endure it. As I said to them on that occasion, in such instances this is one approach which you may think deserves consideration. Where you find governmental assistance necessary in the form of guarantees of investments, of loans or of sales, or assistance in the creation of general conditions which would make operations possible, talk it over with your government. It may not be possible to do all that is asked or even what is asked in any particular circumstance, but may I say that only by your effort as a result of your initiative will your own position in freedom be assured. The activities of other nations in this regard have to be appreciated in this country. The German government assists the manufacturers in that country to obtain markets in the way I have mentioned, and provides jobs for the German people in the process.

speechtext:
I am afraid the hon. member for Cartier, whose advice in this connection I always desire to seek, does not evidence by his question a realization of the magnitude of this problem. I said we were facing a situation where production costs in this country are between 35 and 40 per cent higher than the United States which has a market between 15 and 20 times greater than our own. Surely the hon. member is not suggesting that our flow of immigration should be stepped up so that it would provide a market in this country within a few years of the proportions of the United States market?

We have to look outward. We have to expand our markets abroad. In this way jobs for Canadians may be provided and the benefits of larger production with its lower costs may be made available to the generality of Canadians. The Canadian business, commercial and financial world must go to work for Canada. Let them not be disheartened by those who say that the export of capital in the form of assembly or distributing plants in the form of long term credits for Canadian goods is not possible because Canada is a capital importing country. In the periods of the greatest and most rapid expansion of Great Britain, Great Britain imported capital. But she exported it again in the ways I have mentioned, providing jobs for its people in the process because they understood that there was always capital available for the capable, the industrious and for the stable productive elements in their nation who were willing to use their skills, their initiative and their judgment in its re-export to other areas. There are always some who require the greater stability, the greater security of investment in countries such as ours and who are content that those who use that capital take the greater risks and the greater profits in the export field I have mentioned. This is one side of our nation's aid program which should not be forgotten as we deal with the purely governmental side of our economic and technical assistance to those in the less developed areas.
Another thing I should like to mention is the progress which has been made toward the establishment of an Atlantic institute. I mention that here because if it comes about it is possible that the government will be requested to make a small contribution. I see there will not be time to go into that question. Perhaps on a future occasion we may be able to discuss that particular item. I should like, in closing, to remind the committee of words which are not often quoted now, the words of Alexander Pope:
In Faith and Hope the world will disagree,
But all mankind's concern is Charity:
All must be false that thwart this one great end,
And all of God that bless mankind or mend.

speechtext:
The third meeting of the Canada-United States ministerial committee on joint defence was held at Montebello, Quebec, on July 12 and 13, 1960.
The United States was represented at the meeting by Hon. Robert W. Anderson, secretary of the treasury, Hon. Thomas S. Gates, Jr., secretary of defence, and Hon. Livingston T. Merchant, under-secretary of state for political affairs. Secretary of state Christian A. Herter regretted that developments requiring his personal attention obliged him to cancel his plans to come to the meeting.
Canada was represented by Hon. Howard C. Green, Secretary of State for External Affairs, Hon. Donald M. Fleming, Minister of Finance, Hon. George R. Pearkes, Minister of National Defence and Hon. Raymond J. O'Hurley, Minister of Defence Production.
Ambassador Wigglesworth and Ambassador Heeney with other senior officials of the two governments, were also in attendance.
The committee was established as a result of discussions in July, 1958, in Ottawa between Prime Minister Diefenbaker and President Eisenhower. It was established to consult periodically on all matters affecting the joint defence of Canada and the United States and reviews not only military questions but also the political and economic aspects of joint defence problems.
The members of the committee welcomed the opportunity which this meeting afforded them to have a timely discussion on a broad range of recent international developments of interest and concern to the two governments. They agreed that situations which arise should always be dealt with in a manner which will promote the objectives of the United Nations and contribute to international peace and stability.
By its nature the committee's discussions are largely concerned with matters involving the vital security interest of the two countries.
The committee reviewed the current position concerning negotiations aiming at complete and general disarmament under an
effective system of control. They deplored the recent action of the Soviet union in withdrawing from the 10-nation meetings, thus frustrating its work. The committee agreed that efforts for the resumption of meaningful negotiations must be continued. They were further agreed that pending the achievement of general and controlled disarmament there could be no relaxation of defensive measures.
Particular attention was given to a review of the progress achieved on co-operative measures designed to improve the defences of North America and the committee reaffirmed its conviction that these contribute importantly to the greater strength of collective security within the broader framework of NATO.
The committee reaffirmed the common desire and intention of both governments further to strengthen the north Atlantic alliance and to improve consultation between members within the North Atlantic council, and considered ways and means whereby the alliance's objectives might be achieved in the years ahead.
The committee also reviewed the field of defence production sharing between the two countries. They recognized that this is a long range program. They reaffirmed the concept as one in the best interest of each country and discussed further steps which might be taken to assure a greater measure of co-operation.
The committee noted with satisfaction that the existing machinery for consultation on defence matters between the two countries is operating effectively. It was noted in this respect that the permanent joint board on defence, created by the Ogdensburg declaration of 1940, would this year be completing the twentieth year of its existence and the committee expressed its confidence that the board would continue to play a significant role within the area of its responsibilities.
The date of the next meeting of the committee will be arranged later.
July 13/60.
